R.q:
Amara is preparing a presentation on childhood asthma rates in her state. Her teacher wants students to include one example of each type of source in their bibliographies. Amara has already found a primary source and a secondary source and needs a tertiary source. She has four other items on her desk, gathered from the school library and an online research database.

Which item is a tertiary source?
o: A medical encyclopedia entry that briefly summarizes what asthma is
A review article that compares the results of several asthma studies
A journal article reporting the results of the authors' own survey of parents
A recorded interview in which a researcher describes her asthma study
R.w: Encyclopedias are tertiary sources: they compile and condense information from primary and secondary sources into brief reference entries.

n.1: A review article analyzes and summarizes other researchers' studies, which makes it a secondary source.
n.2: An article reporting the authors' own survey is original research, a primary source.
n.3: A researcher describing her own study firsthand is a primary source.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Every evening at six, Mr. Okafor carried a folding chair to the end of his driveway and sat facing the street until the streetlights came on. Neighbors waved, and he waved back but rarely spoke. On the day a moving truck arrived at the house across the street, he stayed out past dark. The next evening, a young woman from the new family crossed the street with a plate of cookies. Mr. Okafor stood, unfolded a second chair that had been leaning behind his own, and offered it to her.

Which inference about Mr. Okafor is best supported by the passage?
o: He sits outside each evening in order to watch for moving trucks.
He dislikes his longtime neighbors and prefers to be left alone.
He was open to company, though he rarely started conversations himself.
He has been lonely since his wife passed away a short time ago.
R.w: He rarely speaks first, yet he had a second chair ready and offered it as soon as someone approached. Those details support the idea that he welcomed company even though he did not seek it out.

n.0: Distortion: he sits out every evening; the moving truck appeared on one day only.
n.1: Contradicted: he waves back at neighbors and offers the visitor a chair.
n.3: An assumption: the passage never mentions a wife or any loss.

R.q:
Subject: Fire inspection moved to Tuesday
Hi everyone. The fire marshal's visit has moved up from Thursday to Tuesday at 9 a.m. Please have all hallways clear of linen carts and wheelchairs by the end of the Monday evening shift. At our last inspection, we were cited for two blocked exits on the third floor, and the marshal warned that a second citation would bring a fine. I will walk the third floor myself on Monday at 6 p.m. to check the exits. Thank you for your help.
Dana Ruiz, Facilities

Which conclusion is best supported by the email?
o: Dana is especially concerned about the condition of the third floor before Tuesday.
The inspection was moved up because Facilities asked the marshal for an earlier date.
Linen carts may be returned to the hallways once the marshal has left the building.
The fire marshal fined the facility for the two blocked exits on the third floor.
R.w: Dana mentions the earlier third-floor citation, the risk of a fine, and her plan to walk that floor personally on Monday. Together these show special concern about the third floor.

n.1: The email does not say why the date changed; the reason is not given.
n.2: The email says nothing about what happens after the inspection; this is an unsupported assumption.
n.3: The email says a second citation would bring a fine, which means the first citation did not.

R.q:
Read the description of the bar graph.

Title: Prescriptions Filled at Main Street Pharmacy, January to April
Vertical axis: Prescriptions (in hundreds)
Horizontal axis: Month
Bar heights:
January: 32
February: 28
March: 35
April: 30
Note: The pharmacy was closed for two days in February for remodeling. Source: pharmacy records. Each bar counts new prescriptions and refills together. The pharmacy hired a third technician in March to handle the extra work.

According to the graph, how many more prescriptions were filled in March than in February?
R.w: The axis is in hundreds. March (35 hundred = 3,500) minus February (28 hundred = 2,800) is 700 prescriptions.

n.1: Treats the axis as tens instead of hundreds.
n.2: Treats the axis as thousands instead of hundreds.
n.3: Subtracts the bar heights without applying the axis unit of hundreds.

R.q:
When a child has a high fever or a deep cut on a Saturday night, parents in Millbrook have two choices. Urgent care centers treat minor injuries and illnesses, such as sprains, ear infections and cuts that need stitches. Visits typically cost less, and waits are often under an hour. Emergency rooms, on the other hand, are equipped for life-threatening problems such as trouble breathing, seizures or severe bleeding. They are open around the clock but usually cost more and can involve longer waits for less serious cases.

The author most likely uses a compare-and-contrast structure in order to
o: show how emergency rooms have changed over the years.
argue that urgent care centers should replace emergency rooms.
help parents decide which place fits a child's needs.
explain what causes most childhood injuries on weekends.
R.w: Setting the two options side by side (what each treats, cost, wait times, hours) gives parents the information they need to choose between them. The structure serves that practical purpose.

n.0: The passage describes both places as they are now; it gives no history.
n.1: The passage presents emergency rooms as necessary for life-threatening problems, so it does not argue for replacing them.
n.3: Injuries are named as examples of what each place treats; their causes are never discussed.

R.q:
Read the guidelines.

Volunteer Guidelines, Harbor Food Bank
Every new volunteer attends a one-hour orientation before working a first shift. After orientation, volunteers receive a login that lets them sign up for shifts online. Volunteers who wish to drive the delivery van must also show a valid driver's license to the warehouse manager and watch a twenty-minute road-safety video. Van drivers must be at least 21 years old. Shifts that involve lifting boxes heavier than 30 pounds are marked with a star on the online calendar.

Sam has just used his login to sign up online for a starred Saturday shift.

Based on the guidelines, which statement about Sam must be true?
o: Sam is at least 21 years old and has a valid driver's license.
Sam will drive the delivery van during Saturday's shift.
Sam has watched the twenty-minute road-safety video.
Sam has already completed the volunteer orientation.
R.w: Volunteers receive a login after orientation, and Sam used his login to sign up. So he must have completed orientation. The star tells us only that the shift involves heavy lifting.

n.0: The age and license rules apply to van drivers, and nothing says Sam is driving.
n.1: A starred shift means heavy lifting, not driving; nothing says Sam will drive.
n.2: The video is required for van drivers; Sam has signed up for a lifting shift.

R.q:
In January, the cafeteria at Mercy Valley Hospital switched to a new coffee supplier. In February, the number of sick days taken by staff fell by 15 percent compared with January. The cafeteria manager announced that the new coffee is clearly better for staff health and asked the newsletter editor to feature it in the next issue. The manager did not mention that January had been the peak of the local flu season.

Which statement best describes the flaw in the manager's reasoning?
o: It rejects an opposing view by attacking the people who hold that view.
It draws a conclusion about every hospital from one hospital's records.
It assumes that its conclusion is true in order to prove that conclusion.
It assumes that because one event came first, it caused the second one.
R.w: Sick days fell after the coffee changed, so the manager concludes the coffee caused the drop. That is post hoc reasoning, and the end of flu season is a more likely explanation.

n.0: The manager does not respond to any opponent, so there is no personal attack.
n.1: The manager draws a conclusion about this hospital's staff, not about every hospital.
n.2: The manager offers a reason (fewer sick days) that is separate from the conclusion; the flaw is the causal leap.

R.q:
For a pharmacology class, Daniel is gathering sources on a common blood pressure medication. He has found four items in the college library's databases. His instructor asks students to label each source as primary, secondary, or tertiary and reminds them that the label depends on what a source does with information, not on where it is published or how technical it sounds.

Which of Daniel's sources is a secondary source?
o: A journal article reporting a clinical trial the authors ran on the drug
The de-identified records of patients who took part in a drug trial
A review article summarizing the findings of 40 studies on the drug
A pharmacology dictionary that defines the drug class in one entry
R.w: A review article analyzes and summarizes research that others conducted, which makes it a secondary source.

n.0: An article in which researchers report their own original trial is a primary source.
n.1: Patient records are raw data created during the study, so they are primary.
n.3: A dictionary compiles brief information from other sources, so it is tertiary.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Many people assume that a fever is the illness itself and must be brought down right away. In fact, a fever is one of the body's defenses. When the immune system detects an infection, it signals the brain to raise the body's temperature set point. Many bacteria and viruses reproduce less efficiently at higher temperatures, and some immune cells work faster when the body is warmer. For most healthy adults, a moderate fever is uncomfortable but not dangerous. Doctors still advise seeking care for a very high fever, a fever that lasts several days, or any fever in a young infant, because in those cases the underlying cause may need treatment.

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: A fever that lasts several days or occurs in an infant may need a doctor's care.
Some immune cells work faster when the body's temperature rises during illness.
People should bring a fever down quickly to keep an infection from spreading.
A fever is often a helpful defense against infection, not simply an illness to stop.
R.w: The passage opens with a common belief and then corrects it with "In fact, a fever is one of the body's defenses." The rest explains how the fever helps fight infection, with a closing note about when to seek care. The correction is the main idea.

n.0: Too narrow: the closing advice about when to seek care qualifies the main idea rather than stating it.
n.1: Too narrow: faster immune cells are one detail explaining why fever is a defense.
n.2: This is the belief the author sets up in order to correct it, not the author's own point.

R.q:
The Marlow River Bridge will close for repairs on June 1 and stay closed for three months. During the closure, drivers will detour across the Oak Street Bridge, two miles north. When the Marlow bridge closed for one weekend last fall, a traffic study found that travel times across the Oak Street Bridge doubled during morning and evening rush hours, while midday traffic was barely affected. The city has asked large employers to consider flexible start times during the repairs.

Which prediction about the summer is best supported by the passage?
o: Midday trips across the Oak Street Bridge will likely take about double their usual time.
Rush-hour trips across the Oak Street Bridge will likely take longer than usual.
The repairs will last longer than three months because of the heavy detour traffic.
Large employers will require their workers to start later until the bridge reopens.
R.w: The weekend study showed Oak Street travel times doubling at rush hour when the Marlow bridge closed. A three-month closure puts the same cause in motion, so longer rush-hour trips are the supported prediction.

n.0: This uses the wrong part of the study: travel times doubled at rush hour, while midday traffic was barely affected.
n.2: The passage gives no reason to expect the repairs to run over; traffic on the detour does not affect the repair schedule.
n.3: The city only asked employers to consider flexible start times; a requirement is not supported.

R.q:
The two men admitted to Room 412 could not have been more different. Mr. Ortiz, who chatted with every nurse and shared stories about his grandchildren, made friends on the first day. Mr. Hale, by contrast, was reticent, answering most questions with a nod or a single word and turning toward the window when visitors arrived.

As used in the passage, the word reticent most nearly means
o: confused about his care.
unable to hear well.
reluctant to speak.
rude and unfriendly.
R.w: "By contrast" sets Mr. Hale against the talkative Mr. Ortiz, and the details (a nod, a single word) show someone who says little. Reticent means reluctant to speak or reserved.

n.0: His short answers show reserve, not confusion; the passage gives no sign that he misunderstands anything.
n.1: He responds to questions with a nod, which shows he hears them; the contrast is about talkativeness, not hearing.
n.3: Nothing shows hostility; he answers questions, just briefly. "Rude" adds a negative judgment the context does not support.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Heat exhaustion occurs when the body loses too much water and salt, often through heavy sweating during hot weather or hard exercise. Its warning signs include heavy sweating, cool and clammy skin, muscle cramps, nausea, headache and dizziness. A person with heat exhaustion should move to a cooler place, loosen tight clothing and sip water. Heat stroke is more serious. It occurs when the body's temperature rises to 103 degrees Fahrenheit or higher, and the skin may become hot and red, either damp or dry. Heat stroke is an emergency: call 911 and cool the person right away.

According to the passage, which is a warning sign of heat stroke rather than heat exhaustion?
o: Muscle cramps along with nausea
A temperature of 103 degrees or higher
A headache with dizziness and nausea
Cool, clammy skin with heavy sweating
R.w: The passage describes heat stroke as occurring when body temperature reaches 103 degrees Fahrenheit or higher.

n.0: Muscle cramps and nausea are listed as signs of heat exhaustion.
n.2: Headache, dizziness and nausea are listed among the signs of heat exhaustion.
n.3: Cool, clammy skin and heavy sweating are listed as signs of heat exhaustion; heat stroke skin is described as hot and red.

R.q:
In January, trained observers on the fourth-floor medical unit at Bayview Hospital recorded staff cleaning their hands at 412 of 520 required moments, a rate of 79 percent. In late January, the unit installed alcohol gel dispensers beside every bed. The February audit found a rate of 91 percent. The report's author concluded, "The bedside dispensers were the best purchase the hospital made all year."

Which of the following best describes the author's conclusion?
o: It is a fact, because it is based on the measured hand-hygiene rates.
It is an opinion, because it relies on percentages that may be rounded.
It is a fact, because trained observers collected the data for the report.
It is an opinion, because it ranks this purchase above all others.
R.w: The audit rates are facts, but deciding that the dispensers were "the best purchase" of the year is a value judgment that goes beyond the data. Interpreting statistics in this way produces an opinion.

n.0: Facts can support a conclusion without making it a fact. "Best purchase" compares the dispensers to every other purchase, which the data do not measure and which people could judge differently.
n.1: The label is right but the reason is wrong. Rounded percentages are still checkable facts; the statement is an opinion because of the judgment word "best."
n.2: Who collected the data affects how reliable the rates are; it does not turn the author's judgment about the purchase into a fact.

R.q:
Passage 1
Rural school districts struggle to hire teachers, who can often earn more in cities. A four-day school week offers something cities rarely can: a free weekday. It also saves districts money on buses and heating, though the main reason to adopt it is recruiting.

Passage 2
Two years after Pine Hollow District switched to a four-day week, student attendance had stayed about the same. Applications for open teaching jobs doubled. In a survey, many parents reported paying more for child care on the fifth day.

Which detail from Passage 2 best supports the main claim of Passage 1?
o: Student attendance stayed about the same after the switch.
Many parents reported higher child care costs on the fifth day.
Four-day weeks save districts money on buses and heating.
Applications for open teaching jobs doubled after the switch.
R.w: Passage 1's main claim is that a four-day week helps rural districts recruit teachers. Doubled teaching applications in Pine Hollow is direct evidence for that claim.

n.0: Stable attendance is a real finding, but it does not address teacher recruitment.
n.1: Higher child care costs are a drawback and do nothing to support the recruiting claim.
n.2: This detail comes from Passage 1, not Passage 2, and it is a side benefit rather than the main claim.

R.q:
Read the passage.

At a town meeting on the proposed walking trail, three speakers addressed the council. Parks director Helen Moore said the trail would cost about $1.2 million, mostly paid for by a state grant, and could open within two years. Dr. Kevin Asante, a family physician, argued that the trail would give residents a safe place to exercise and noted that many of his patients live more than a mile from any park. Business owner Lydia Chen supported the trail but asked the council to add parking near the downtown end, saying that trail users would otherwise fill the spaces her customers need. The council agreed to vote on the plan next month.

Which statement accurately reports what a speaker said?
o: Ms. Chen opposed the trail because it would take parking from her customers.
Ms. Moore said that the trail would be paid for mostly by local property taxes.
Dr. Asante said that many of his patients live more than a mile from a park.
Dr. Asante asked the council to add parking near the downtown end of the trail.
R.w: The passage reports that Dr. Asante noted that many of his patients live more than a mile from any park.

n.0: Ms. Chen supported the trail; she asked for added parking rather than opposing the plan.
n.1: Ms. Moore said the trail would be paid for mostly by a state grant, not local taxes.
n.3: Wrong speaker: the parking request came from Ms. Chen, not Dr. Asante.

R.q:
Read the passage.

When a caller dials 911 in Harlan County, the call first rings at the county's emergency communications center, where a call-taker answers. Before asking about the emergency, the call-taker confirms the caller's location, because a dropped call is useless if no one knows where to go. The call-taker then asks what happened and types the answers into a computer system, which suggests a priority level. A dispatcher, seated at a separate console, reads the entry and radios the nearest available ambulance. While the ambulance is on its way, the call-taker stays on the line and gives the caller first-aid instructions.

Place the steps in the order in which they occur, starting with the first.
o: The call-taker confirms the caller's location
The call-taker asks what happened and enters the answers
The call-taker gives the caller first-aid instructions
The dispatcher radios the nearest available ambulance
The call rings at the emergency communications center
R.w: The call reaches the center and is answered; location is confirmed "before asking about the emergency"; the details are then entered; the dispatcher reads the entry and sends an ambulance; and first-aid instructions come "while the ambulance is on its way."

R.q:
How to use your inhaler
This medicine works best when it reaches deep into your lungs. Breathe out fully, seal your lips around the mouthpiece, and press the canister as you begin a slow, deep breath. Then hold your breath for 10 seconds. If you breathe in quickly, much of the medicine lands on the back of your throat instead of reaching your lungs, and over time you may notice a hoarse voice. Rinse your mouth with water after each use to remove any medicine left in your mouth.

Devon presses the canister and then takes a quick, sharp breath each time he uses his inhaler. Based on the leaflet, what is most likely to happen?
o: Less of the medicine will reach his lungs, and his voice may become hoarse.
The medicine will reach his lungs faster and so begin to work sooner.
He will need to hold his breath longer than 10 seconds to make up for it.
Rinsing his mouth will carry the medicine from his throat to his lungs.
R.w: The leaflet says a quick breath leaves much of the medicine on the back of the throat instead of in the lungs and may cause a hoarse voice over time.

n.1: This reverses the leaflet: a quick breath sends less medicine to the lungs, not more.
n.2: The leaflet offers no longer breath-hold as a fix; the fix it implies is a slow, deep breath.
n.3: The leaflet says rinsing removes medicine left in the mouth; it does not move medicine to the lungs.

R.q:
Read the directions.

Testing Your Well Water for Bacteria
1. Wash your hands. Do not touch the inside of the bottle or cap.
2. Remove the aerator (screen) from the end of the kitchen faucet.
3. Run cold water for 5 minutes.
4. Before filling, check that the white powder is still inside the bottle. Do not rinse it out.
5. Fill the bottle to the 100 mL line, not to the top.
6. Cap tightly and write the date and time of collection on the label.
7. Keep the sample cold and deliver it to the lab within 24 hours.

According to the directions, what should a person do immediately after running the cold water for 5 minutes?
o: Check that the white powder is still in the bottle
Remove the aerator from the end of the faucet
Fill the bottle with water up to the 100 mL line
Rinse the bottle out with the cold running water
R.w: Running the water is step 3. Step 4, checking that the powder is still in the bottle, comes next and must happen before filling.

n.1: Removing the aerator is step 2, which comes before running the water.
n.2: Filling is step 5; choosing it skips the powder check in step 4.
n.3: The directions say not to rinse the bottle, since that would remove the powder.

R.q:
When Rosa Jimenez, 58, felt a sudden ache in her jaw while gardening, she assumed she had pulled a muscle. Two hours later, she was in a cardiac unit. Rosa's experience is common. Women having a heart attack often notice symptoms other than chest pain, such as jaw or back pain, nausea, shortness of breath or unusual fatigue. Because these symptoms are less familiar, women often wait longer than men before seeking care. Doctors advise anyone with these symptoms to call 911 rather than drive to the hospital.

Why does the author most likely begin the passage with Rosa Jimenez's experience?
o: to show that jaw pain is the most common symptom in women
to entertain readers with a dramatic story
to draw readers in with a real example of the problem
to argue that gardening is risky for older adults
R.w: The anecdote puts a human face on the problem the passage goes on to explain: women's heart attack symptoms are often missed. An opening story in an informational text usually serves to engage the reader and introduce the topic.

n.0: Jaw pain is listed as one of several possible symptoms; the passage does not rank it as the most common.
n.1: The story is dramatic, but it introduces factual health information; the passage as a whole informs rather than entertains.
n.3: Gardening is simply what Rosa was doing; the passage never suggests that gardening caused her heart attack.

R.q:
Last month, Lakeside Medical Center raised its parking fee for visitors to $28 a day. Families sitting at the bedsides of seriously ill loved ones, many of whom visit every day for weeks, now pay more than $800 a month simply to be present. The hospital made the change without a single public notice. This is an outrage, and the board owes these families an explanation and a refund.

Which word best describes the author's tone toward the hospital's decision?
o: resigned
indignant
sympathetic
sarcastic
R.w: "An outrage" and the demand for an explanation and a refund express anger at something the author considers unjust. Angry protest at an unfair act is an indignant tone.

n.0: "Resigned" means accepting something unwelcome as unavoidable, but the author demands that the board act.
n.2: The author does show sympathy, but toward the families. The question asks about the tone toward the hospital's decision, which is angry, not sympathetic.
n.3: Sarcasm says the opposite of what is meant; the author states the complaint directly.

R.q:
The night before my first clinical shift, I laid out my scrubs, packed my stethoscope and set three alarms. When I walked onto the unit at 6:45 a.m., the charge nurse looked up from her computer. "You must be the new student," she said. "You'll be with Marcus today. Stick close to him, ask questions, and don't touch any pumps unless he says so." I nodded and tried to look calmer than I felt. My hands were shaking as I followed Marcus down the hall.

From which point of view is the passage narrated?
o: third person omniscient
third person limited
first person
second person
R.w: The narrator takes part in the events and refers to herself as "I" and "my" throughout. That is first-person narration.

n.0: An omniscient narrator reports every character's thoughts; this narrator reports only her own feelings and what others say aloud.
n.1: A third-person narrator stands outside the story and uses "he" or "she" for the main character; this narrator is the main character.
n.3: "You" appears only inside the charge nurse's dialogue. Pronouns in quoted speech do not set the narrator's point of view.

R.q:
Passage 1
In 1816, the French physician Rene Laennec needed to listen to a patient's heart but felt uncomfortable pressing his ear to her chest. He rolled a few sheets of paper into a tube, placed one end on her chest, and was surprised by how clearly he could hear. He later built a wooden version and called it a stethoscope.

Passage 2
Hear what you have been missing. The ClearBeat Digital Stethoscope amplifies heart and lung sounds up to 40 times and filters out room noise. Record sounds, share them with colleagues, and replay them in slow motion. Order today and receive a free carrying case.

Which statement best describes how the purposes of the passages differ?
o: Both passages mainly explain the way that a stethoscope makes sounds louder for doctors.
Passage 1 informs readers about the device's origin; Passage 2 urges readers to buy one.
Passage 1 argues for older stethoscopes; Passage 2 informs about recording heart sounds.
Passage 1 entertains with a personal story; Passage 2 explains how digital sound works.
R.w: Passage 1 is a short history of how the stethoscope was invented. Passage 2 is an advertisement with a call to action (Order today) and an offer, so its purpose is to persuade.

n.0: Passage 1 tells how the device was invented, and Passage 2 sells a product; neither mainly explains amplification.
n.2: Passage 1 makes no argument for older devices; it simply recounts the invention.
n.3: Passage 1 uses an anecdote, but to inform about history; and Passage 2 sells a product rather than explaining technology.

R.q:
Timeline: Harbor Street Clinic
1998 | Clinic opens with two exam rooms
2004 | Dental services added
2011 | Clinic moves to a larger building on Pier Avenue
2016 | Evening hours begin
2021 | Telehealth visits begin

From the clinic's anniversary newsletter: The year after the clinic moved, it hired its first full-time Spanish interpreter. Two years after hiring the interpreter, it started a diabetes education class. The class became so popular that a second weekly session was added in the same year that evening hours began.

Based on the timeline and the newsletter, in what year did the diabetes education class start?
R.w: Step 1: the clinic moved in 2011 (timeline), so the interpreter was hired in 2012. Step 2: the class started two years after the hire, in 2014.

n.0: 2016 is when evening hours began and the second session was added, not when the class started.
n.1: 2013 counts two years from the move (2011) instead of from the interpreter's hiring (2012).
n.2: 2012 is the year the interpreter was hired, one step early.

R.q:
Read the passage.

For years I believed I was simply bad at math. In high school I copied formulas onto index cards, memorized them the night before tests, and forgot them by the following week. When I enrolled in a nursing prerequisite course at twenty-eight, the instructor, Ms. Reyes, refused to hand out formulas to memorize. Instead she made us work out dosage problems with real medicine labels and explain each step aloud to a partner. The first month was miserable. By the final exam, though, I could set up a problem I had never seen before, and I realized I could not remember the last time I had written a formula on a card.

Which conclusion about the narrator is best supported by the passage?
o: The narrator's earlier struggles came from memorizing rather than understanding.
The narrator still prefers to memorize formulas on index cards before a test.
The narrator went on to earn the highest score in the prerequisite course.
The narrator found the course easy from the start because of Ms. Reyes's methods.
R.w: The narrator once memorized and quickly forgot formulas and believed they were bad at math. After learning to reason through problems and explain each step, the narrator could solve unfamiliar problems. The contrast suggests the earlier trouble came from the study method, not a lack of ability.

n.1: Opposite of the passage: the narrator no longer writes formulas on cards.
n.2: Unsupported: the passage says the narrator could solve new problems, not how the narrator ranked.
n.3: Contradicted: the narrator says the first month was miserable.

R.q:
Read the price table.

Riverbend Fitness Membership Options
Plan | Monthly fee | Joining fee | Includes
Basic | $25 | $50 | Gym floor, 5 a.m. to 9 p.m.
Plus | $40 | $50 | Gym floor 24 hours, group classes
Family (up to 4 people) | $70 | none | Plus benefits for each member
Student (with school ID) | $20 | none | Basic benefits
Members age 65 and older pay 20 percent less than the listed monthly fee for any plan. Joining fees are not discounted.

Carmen is 67 years old. She wants a membership for herself that includes group classes. Based on the table, what will her monthly fee be?
R.w: Group classes come with the Plus plan ($40 a month). Carmen is over 65, so she pays 20 percent less: $40 - $8 = $32.

n.0: $40 is the Plus fee before the senior discount.
n.1: $56 is the discounted Family plan, which is for up to four people; Carmen needs a membership for herself.
n.2: $20 is the Basic plan with the senior discount ($25 - $5), and Basic does not include group classes.

R.q:
The night shift on 6 North began quietly. A cold rain streaked the windows, and the hallway lights hummed overhead. At the nurses' station, an old coffee maker grumbled its way through one more pot. By midnight, the call lights were blinking at a steady pace, and Nurse Diaz had already walked what felt like ten miles.

Which phrase from the passage is an example of personification?
o: the hallway lights hummed overhead
walked what felt like ten miles
grumbled its way through one more pot
the call lights were blinking at a steady pace
R.w: To grumble is a human action (complaining in a low, irritated voice). Giving the coffee maker this human behavior is personification.

n.0: Lights and machines literally hum; this describes a real sound, not a human action.
n.1: This is hyperbole, an exaggeration of how far she walked, not a human trait given to an object.
n.3: Call lights really do blink; this is a literal description of the signals, not a human trait given to an object.

R.q:
Read the directions.

Assembling the Shower Chair
Wait until the backrest is secure before you attach the four legs to the seat frame. Before you attach the backrest, slide the two rubber grips onto the armrests. The armrests themselves must be bolted to the seat frame before any other step, since the backrest screws pass through them. Once the legs are on, set the chair's height by pressing the push pins into matching holes on all four legs. Test the chair on a flat surface before use.

Place the assembly steps in the order the directions require, starting with the first.
o: Slide the rubber grips onto the armrests
Set the height with the push pins
Attach the backrest
Attach the four legs
Bolt the armrests to the seat frame
R.w: The armrests are bolted on before any other step because the backrest screws pass through them. The grips go on before the backrest. The legs wait until the backrest is secure, and the height is set once the legs are on.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a public health official: Sugary drinks are the largest single source of added sugar in American diets. When the price of a product rises, people buy less of it. A tax of two cents per ounce would lower consumption and fund school nutrition programs.

Passage 2
From a community organizer: A soda tax takes the biggest bite from families who are already stretched thin, since they spend a larger share of their income on groceries. If we want people to drink fewer sugary drinks, we should fund clean water stations in parks and nutrition classes in schools.

Which assumption do the two authors share?
o: Low-income families buy more sugary drinks than other families.
A tax is the most effective way to cut sugary drink consumption.
Lowering sugary drink consumption would benefit public health.
Nutrition classes in schools have had little effect on habits.
R.w: The official proposes a tax to lower consumption, and the organizer says "if we want people to drink fewer sugary drinks" and offers other methods. Both take for granted that less consumption is desirable.

n.0: The organizer says lower-income families spend a larger share of income on groceries, not that they buy more soda.
n.1: This is the official's position; the organizer rejects the tax in favor of other approaches.
n.3: The organizer recommends nutrition classes, and the official does not discuss them.

R.q:
The Main Street Farmers Market has operated every summer since 2018. Supporters say it has transformed downtown. In its best season, 2022, the market drew 48,000 visitors, and nearby shops reported their strongest summer sales in a decade. Vendors praise the friendly crowds and the shaded location along the river. Clearly, the market is a success that deserves a permanent city subsidy of $75,000 a year.

Which feature of the passage most strongly suggests a biased presentation?
o: It reports figures from the market's best year and omits the others.
It includes specific numbers about visitors and the size of the subsidy.
It states the author's conclusion in the final sentence of the passage.
It describes vendors' opinions about the crowds and the location.
R.w: The market has run for several seasons, yet the author reports figures from only its best one. Choosing the most favorable data while leaving out the rest (cherry-picking) gives a one-sided picture and signals bias.

n.1: Specific numbers can make a passage more balanced, not less. The problem is which numbers were chosen, not that numbers appear.
n.2: Placing a conclusion at the end is a structural choice that any writer, biased or not, might make.
n.3: Reporting what vendors say is a normal way to add detail; it does not by itself slant the presentation.

R.q:
Read the description of the flowchart.

Flowchart: Front Desk Check-In
Start: "Does the patient have an appointment today?"
If NO, go to: "Is the patient having chest pain or trouble breathing?" If YES: "Send to the emergency department." If NO: "Offer the next walk-in slot."
If YES, go to: "Is the patient more than 15 minutes late?" If YES: "Offer to reschedule the appointment." If NO: "Verify insurance," then "Send to the waiting room."

A patient who has an appointment arrives 20 minutes late. She has no chest pain or trouble breathing. According to the flowchart, what should the receptionist do?
o: Offer her the next available walk-in slot
Send her to the emergency department
Offer to reschedule her appointment
Verify her insurance and send her to the waiting room
R.w: She has an appointment, so follow the YES branch to the lateness question. She is 20 minutes late, which is more than 15, so the chart says to offer to reschedule.

n.0: The walk-in slot is on the branch for patients without an appointment.
n.1: The emergency department branch is for patients without an appointment who have chest pain or trouble breathing.
n.3: This is the path for a patient who is 15 minutes late or less.

R.q:
This year, Monroe Elementary began serving free breakfast in the cafeteria from 7:30 to 7:55 a.m. The principal reports that students who ate the school breakfast at least three times a week missed an average of 4 days of school, while students who did not eat it missed an average of 9 days. She concludes that the breakfast program improves attendance and plans to ask the district to expand it.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the principal's conclusion?
o: Students driven to school arrive in time for breakfast, but most bus riders arrive after it ends.
The breakfast program serves whole-grain cereal, low-fat milk, and fresh fruit to students each morning.
Teachers report that students who eat the school breakfast are less restless during morning classes.
Attendance improved most among the students who ate breakfast at school on every single school day.
R.w: If breakfast eaters are mostly students who are driven to school, a difference in families or transportation, rather than the breakfast, could explain the attendance gap. An alternative explanation weakens a causal conclusion.

n.1: The menu describes the program but does not affect whether it caused better attendance.
n.2: This supports a different benefit (behavior) and does not undercut the attendance claim.
n.3: More breakfast linked to more improvement is a dose pattern that supports the principal's conclusion.

R.q:
Rosa had worked weekend shifts at the hardware store since March, and every paycheck went into an envelope marked CAR. She had already turned down a beach trip in June and skipped the new phone that her friends all bought. By August, the envelope held $2,600 of the $3,000 her uncle was asking for his old sedan. On Friday, her friend Tasha called with news: she had two spare tickets to a concert in the city on Saturday, $150 each, and she wanted Rosa to come.

Based on the passage, how will Rosa most likely respond to Tasha's offer?
o: She will ask Tasha to lend her the money until her next paycheck arrives.
She will turn down the ticket so that she can keep saving for the car.
She will buy the ticket and ask her uncle to lower his price for the sedan.
She will accept the ticket because she has nearly reached her savings goal.
R.w: Rosa has repeatedly given up treats (a beach trip, a new phone) to save for the car and is still $400 short. Her established pattern points to declining the $150 ticket.

n.0: Borrowing from Tasha has no basis in the text and runs against her habit of saving every paycheck.
n.2: This needs an event the passage never suggests: nothing indicates the uncle would change his price.
n.3: Being close to the goal does not reverse her pattern; she is still $400 short, and nothing suggests she would stop saving now.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Start with the word HOSPITAL. Carry out the steps below in order, applying each step to the result of the step before it.
1. Remove the second letter.
2. Replace every vowel (A, E, I, O, U) with the letter that comes immediately after it in the alphabet.
3. Move the last letter to the front of the word.
4. Reverse the order of all the letters.
5. Insert the letter R between the third and fourth letters.

Which of the following is the final result?
o: BTJRPSHL
BTRJPSHL
BTJPSHL
LBTRJPSH
R.w: HOSPITAL, step 1: HSPITAL. Step 2 (I to J, A to B): HSPJTBL. Step 3: LHSPJTB. Step 4: BTJPSHL. Step 5, R between the third letter (J) and the fourth (P): BTJRPSHL.

n.1: Off by one: the R was placed between the second and third letters.
n.2: This is the result after step 4; step 5's inserted R is missing.
n.3: Step 3 was skipped: reversing HSPJTBL gives LBTJPSH, and inserting R gives LBTRJPSH.

R.q:
Read the passage.

In a growing number of counties, paramedics spend part of their shifts visiting patients at home rather than waiting for emergency calls. These community paramedicine programs focus on people who call 911 often or who were recently discharged from the hospital. During a visit, a paramedic may check blood pressure, review a patient's medicine bottles for duplicates, and look for hazards such as loose rugs. One county program reported that frequent callers enrolled for six months made about half as many 911 calls as before. Programs are often funded by grants, and some counties have struggled to keep them running when the grants end. Even so, supporters see home visits as a way to treat small problems before they become emergencies.

The main idea of the passage is that community paramedicine programs use home visits to head off emergencies. Which details from the passage support this main idea? Select all that apply.
o: Paramedics review patients' medicine bottles for duplicates.
Paramedics check patients' homes for hazards such as loose rugs.
Enrolled frequent callers made about half as many 911 calls.
Some counties have struggled to keep their programs running.
Paramedics visit patients in the hospital before discharge.
Programs are often paid for with grants that can run out.
R.w: A supporting detail shows how or that home visits prevent emergencies. Checking for duplicate medicines and for fall hazards are preventive actions, and the drop in 911 calls is evidence that the visits head off emergencies.

n.3: Struggling to keep programs running is a drawback the author concedes, not support for the main idea.
n.4: Distortion: the passage describes home visits to people already discharged, not hospital visits before discharge.
n.5: Grant funding is about how programs are paid for, a limitation rather than support for the idea that visits prevent emergencies.

R.q:
Dr. Nadia Hassan studied the X-ray for a long moment. She was almost sure the fracture would need surgery, but she wanted the orthopedic team to confirm it before she said anything to the family. In the waiting room, Mr. Brooks paced between the vending machine and the window, checking his phone every few seconds. His daughter sat with her arm in a sling, staring at the floor. When Dr. Hassan finally walked in, she smiled and said, "Let's talk about next steps."

Which point of view does the author use in the passage?
o: first person
third person omniscient
third person limited
third person objective
R.w: The narrator uses "she" and reports Dr. Hassan's private thoughts (she was almost sure about surgery, she wanted confirmation). Mr. Brooks and his daughter are shown only through their actions. Access to one character's mind is third person limited.

n.0: The narrator never says "I"; the only first-person words would be in dialogue, and there are none.
n.1: An omniscient narrator would reveal what Mr. Brooks and his daughter were thinking. Here we see only their actions.
n.3: An objective narrator reports only actions and speech, but this narrator tells us Dr. Hassan's thoughts.

R.q:
Parents often warn children that reading in dim light will ruin their eyesight. Eye doctors say this belief is mistaken. Reading in poor light can make the eyes feel tired and dry and may bring on a headache, but these effects go away after rest and leave no lasting damage. Nearsightedness, which has become more common among children, is linked to family history and to spending little time outdoors.

Which statement would the author identify as a misconception?
o: Reading in dim light causes lasting harm to eyesight.
Eye strain from poor lighting goes away with rest.
Reading in dim light can make the eyes feel tired.
Nearsightedness is linked to spending little time outdoors.
R.w: The passage presents the warning that dim light "will ruin" eyesight as a widely held belief that eye doctors say is mistaken, because the effects are temporary. That makes it a misconception.

n.1: The author states this directly as fact to explain why no lasting damage occurs.
n.2: The author accepts this as true; tired, dry eyes are named as a real short-term effect.
n.3: The author presents this link as accurate information about the real causes of nearsightedness.

R.q:
Andre has just been assigned a group project on sickle cell disease, a topic he knows little about. Before he reads the detailed research articles his group has collected, he wants a short, reliable overview of what the disease is, how it is inherited, and its main symptoms, so that he can follow the technical terms in those articles. His group meets on Thursday to divide up the reading.

Which source would best serve Andre's purpose?
o: A patient's blog about daily life with sickle cell disease
A current medical encyclopedia entry on sickle cell disease
An article reporting a new gene therapy trial in 40 patients
A news story about a fundraising walk for sickle cell research
R.w: A current encyclopedia entry is a tertiary source designed to give a broad, reliable overview of a topic, which is exactly what Andre needs before reading detailed research.

n.0: A personal blog gives one person's experience, not a reliable overview of the disease.
n.2: A single trial report is primary research on one narrow question and assumes the background Andre lacks.
n.3: A story about a fundraiser does not explain the disease, its inheritance, or symptoms.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Caring for Your New Cast
For the first 48 hours, keep the injured arm raised above the level of your heart as much as possible to reduce swelling. A plaster cast takes about 48 hours to harden fully, while a fiberglass cast hardens in about 30 minutes. Keep either type dry: cover it with a plastic bag when bathing, and do not hold the cast under running water. If the cast gets damp, dry it with a hair dryer on the cool setting. Do not push objects inside the cast to scratch an itch. Call your doctor if your fingers turn blue or cold, if you cannot move them, or if the cast still feels too tight after the first 48 hours.

According to the passage, what should a patient do if the cast gets damp?
o: Cover it with a plastic bag and keep the arm raised
Wait 48 hours for the cast to harden again
Call the doctor so that the cast can be checked
Dry it with a hair dryer on the cool setting
R.w: The passage states: "If the cast gets damp, dry it with a hair dryer on the cool setting."

n.0: The plastic bag is for keeping the cast dry while bathing, and raising the arm is for swelling; neither is the step for a damp cast.
n.1: 48 hours is how long a plaster cast takes to harden at first; the passage does not say a damp cast needs to reharden.
n.2: The reasons to call the doctor are blue or cold fingers, inability to move them, or tightness after 48 hours, not dampness.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a hospital administrator: Last year we ended fixed visiting hours. Families may now visit at any time, because patients with loved ones nearby report less anxiety and often understand their discharge plans better. To protect rest, we allow two visitors at a time after 9 p.m.

Passage 2
From a nurse's blog: Open visiting has helped many of my patients, and I would not go back. But on night shift, a crowded room can keep a patient awake and slow down care. Hospitals that welcome families should also set quiet hours that visitors respect.

On which point do the two authors agree?
o: Patients recover faster when visitors come during daytime hours.
Nighttime visitors should be limited to two people per patient.
Family presence helps patients, but nighttime visits need some limits.
Open visiting adds to the workload of nurses on the night shift.
R.w: The administrator credits family presence with less anxiety and caps night visitors at two; the nurse says open visiting has helped and calls for quiet hours. Both support families while limiting nights.

n.0: Neither passage compares daytime and nighttime visits for recovery speed.
n.1: The two-visitor rule appears in Passage 1 only; the nurse proposes quiet hours, not a number.
n.3: Slower care at night is the nurse's concern in Passage 2; the administrator does not discuss workload.

R.q:
Oral and tympanic thermometers are both common in clinics. An oral thermometer is placed under the tongue and takes about 10 to 40 seconds to give a reading, depending on the model. A tympanic thermometer, by contrast, reads the temperature inside the ear in one to two seconds. Both give reliable results when used correctly. However, oral readings can be thrown off if a patient has just had a hot or cold drink, whereas tympanic readings can be affected by earwax or a poorly placed probe.

Which organizational structure does the author use?
o: chronological order
description
classification into types
compare and contrast
R.w: The passage sets two thermometers side by side, noting similarities ("both") and differences ("by contrast," "however," "whereas"). That is compare-and-contrast structure.

n.0: Times appear (seconds per reading), but the passage does not narrate events or steps in order.
n.1: Each thermometer is described, but the descriptions are arranged to show how the two are alike and different, which makes the structure comparative.
n.2: Classification sorts many items into categories; this passage weighs two specific devices against each other.

R.q:
When my grandmother broke her hip, the nearest rehabilitation center was two hours away, and our family could visit only on Sundays. Rural counties like ours need small rehab units attached to local hospitals. Patients recover better when family members can visit often, according to a review of 22 studies on stroke and hip-fracture recovery. Some health officials argue that small units cannot afford specialized staff. But traveling therapists already rotate among rural hospitals in neighboring counties, and the state could fund the same model here. Write to your state representative this week.

Which statement best describes how the argument is organized?
o: A story introduces a claim, which is supported, challenged, and then defended.
A claim is stated, and the author changes position after weighing an objection.
A problem is described in detail, and the author declines to propose a remedy.
Two opposing views receive equal weight, and readers are left to decide.
R.w: The grandmother's story leads to the claim (rural rehab units), followed by evidence (the 22-study review), an objection (staffing costs), a rebuttal (traveling therapists), and a call to action.

n.1: The author answers the objection with traveling therapists and keeps the original position.
n.2: The author proposes rehab units and a state-funded therapist model.
n.3: The author clearly takes one side and urges readers to act on it.

R.q:
Read the paragraph.

(1) Children who go to bed at the same time each night tend to fall asleep faster. (2) A steady bedtime helps set the body's internal clock, which controls when a child begins to feel drowsy. (3) Researchers have linked regular bedtimes to better attention and behavior in school. (4) Teenagers' internal clocks shift later, which is why many feel alert late at night. (5) Even on weekends, keeping bedtime within an hour of the weekday time helps the clock stay steady. (6) Families that build a short routine, such as a bath, a book and lights out, often find that bedtime battles become less frequent.

The main idea of the paragraph is that a consistent bedtime benefits children. Which sentence does NOT support this main idea?
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
Sentence 5
R.w: Sentence 4 shares a key phrase (internal clock) with the paragraph, but it describes a natural shift in teenagers' clocks, not a benefit of a consistent bedtime for children. The other listed sentences each explain, show or extend that benefit.

n.0: Sentence 3 gives evidence of a benefit: better attention and behavior in school.
n.2: Sentence 2 explains how a steady bedtime helps, by setting the internal clock that controls drowsiness.
n.3: Sentence 5 explains how to keep the benefit on weekends, so it supports the idea of a consistent bedtime.

R.q:
Last winter, a volunteer found a gray terrier curled in a roadside ditch, too weak to lift his head. We named him Biscuit. For three weeks, our staff fed him by hand every four hours and wrapped him in warm towels while he shivered through the nights. This morning, Biscuit trotted out the front door with his new family, tail wagging. Our shelter cares for about 400 animals a year. Every Biscuit begins with a donor like you. Please give today.

The author mainly tries to persuade readers by appealing to their
o: sense of logic, through data on the shelter's yearly costs
trust, through the shelter director's professional credentials
sense of duty, by comparing the shelter with other shelters
emotions, through a vivid story about a single rescued dog
R.w: Most of the letter tells Biscuit's story in moving detail (too weak to lift his head, shivering, tail wagging) before asking for money. That is mainly an appeal to emotion (pathos).

n.0: One figure appears (about 400 animals a year), but no cost data, and the story carries the appeal.
n.1: The letter never names its author's role or credentials.
n.2: No other shelters are mentioned.

R.q:
Read the news brief.

The Fairmont City Council approved a new bike-share program on Tuesday, two weeks after a public hearing at which more than sixty residents spoke. The hearing itself had been scheduled after a petition with 4,000 signatures reached the mayor's office in March. Under the plan, bikes will appear at 40 stations by June, following a month-long test with city employees in May. Riders will pay $1 to unlock a bike and 15 cents per minute.

According to the news brief, which of these events happened first?
o: The city council approved the bike-share program.
A petition with 4,000 signatures reached the mayor.
More than sixty residents spoke at a public hearing.
City employees began testing the bikes in May.
R.w: The hearing was scheduled after the petition arrived in March, and the council vote came two weeks after the hearing. The employee test is planned for later. So the petition came first, even though it is mentioned after the vote.

n.0: Order of mention trap: the vote is mentioned first but came two weeks after the hearing.
n.2: The hearing was scheduled after the petition reached the mayor.
n.3: The May test is a future step, after the council's approval.

R.q:
A school district surveyed 1,200 high school students about sleep. Students who used their phones in bed after 10 p.m. reported sleeping about 50 minutes less on school nights than students who did not, even though both groups reported going to bed at similar times. The district then launched a campaign urging families to charge phones outside the bedroom. Early results from 80 families who joined a trial of the campaign show that the students fell asleep about 20 minutes sooner on average.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Students who use phones in bed go to bed later than students who do not use them.
Students who join the campaign can expect to gain about 50 minutes of sleep on school nights.
Phone use in bed may delay sleep even when students go to bed at the same time as their peers.
Most high school students in the district probably use their phones in bed after 10 p.m.
R.w: Both groups went to bed at similar times, yet phone users slept about 50 minutes less, and removing phones helped trial students fall asleep sooner. Together these details support the idea that phone use delays falling asleep.

n.0: This contradicts the passage, which says both groups reported going to bed at similar times.
n.1: This over-extends the data: 50 minutes was the survey gap, but the trial showed students falling asleep about 20 minutes sooner.
n.3: The passage gives no share of students who use phones in bed, so a majority cannot be concluded.

M.q: To qualify for an honors program, Jordan needs a mean score of at least 85 on five exams. Jordan's first four scores are 78, 91, 84, and 88. What is the lowest score Jordan can earn on the fifth exam and still qualify?

tr.85: the target mean, not the needed score
tr.85.25: the mean of the first four scores

M.w: Total needed = mean x count = 85 x 5 = 425. Current total = 78 + 91 + 84 + 88 = 341. Fifth score = 425 - 341 = 84.

M.q: A medication is given every 6 hours. The first dose was given at 2140 (24-hour clock). At what time is the third dose due, in 12-hour time?
M.w: Second dose: 2140 + 6 h = 0340. Third dose: 0340 + 6 h = 0940, which is 9:40 a.m. The third dose comes two intervals (12 hours) after the first.

n.0: 3:40 a.m. (0340) is the second dose.
n.2: 3:40 p.m. adds three 6-hour intervals (18 h); the third dose is only two intervals after the first.
n.3: 0940 is before noon, so it is 9:40 a.m.; 9:40 p.m. would be written 2140.

M.q: A clinic waiting room has a circular rug with a diameter of 8 feet. The staff want to know how much floor space the rug covers. What is the area of the rug? Use 3.14 for pi.

n.0: 25.12 is the circumference (3.14 × 8), a length rather than an area.
n.2: This multiplies pi by the radius (3.14 × 4) instead of by the radius squared.
n.3: This uses the diameter (8 ft) as the radius; r = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 ft.

M.q: Four race times, in minutes, are listed in different forms. Which list shows the times in descending order (greatest to least)?

n.0: 2.205 is less than 2 1/4 = 2.250, so it must come after 2 1/4.
n.1: This list is in ascending order (least to greatest), the reverse of what is asked.
n.3: 2.205 is not the greatest; having more digits does not make a decimal larger (2.205 < 2.3).

M.q: A health survey reports that 22.5% of adults in a county walk to work at least once a week. Which fraction, in lowest terms, is equivalent to 22.5%?

n.0: 1/4 = 25%. It rounds 22.5% to 25% before converting, which changes the value.
n.2: 9/400 = 0.0225, which is 2.25%. The decimal point was moved one place too far.
n.3: 9/4 = 2.25. This writes the percent over 10 instead of 100.

M.q: A 12-ounce bag of coffee makes 45 cups. At the same rate, how many cups can be made from a 32-ounce bag? Enter the number of cups.

tr.65: Added the 20-ounce difference to 45 instead of scaling.
tr.8.53: Set up the second ratio upside down (12 × 32 ÷ 45).

M.w: Set up 12/45 = 32/c. Cross-multiply: 12c = 1,440, so c = 120 cups.

M.q: A survey of 25 households records the number of children in each: 0 children, 4 households; 1 child, 7 households; 2 children, 8 households; 3 children, 4 households; 4 children, 2 households. What is the mean number of children per household? Enter your answer as a decimal.

tr.2: the median or mode, not the mean
tr.5: the mean of the household counts (25 / 5)
tr.8.6: 43 / 5, dividing by the number of categories instead of households

M.q: A safety data sheet lists the storage temperature of a laboratory reagent as 298 kelvins. Use K = °C + 273. The lab's thermostat displays degrees Fahrenheit. What is the storage temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?

n.1: This changes to 25 °C correctly but then multiplies by 5/9 instead of 9/5 before adding 32.
n.2: This adds 32 to 25 °C without first multiplying by 9/5.
n.3: 25 is the temperature in degrees Celsius; it still has to be converted to °F.

M.q: On Monday a checking account was at -45 dollars, and on Tuesday it was at 30 dollars. Which expression gives the distance between -45 and 30 on a number line?
M.w: Distance between a and b is |b - a|: |30 - (-45)| = |30 + 45| = 75.

n.0: |30| - |-45| = 30 - 45 = -15; a difference of absolute values is not the distance.
n.2: 30 - 45 = -15 drops the negative sign of -45 and gives a negative distance.
n.3: |30 + (-45)| = 15 adds the numbers instead of subtracting them.

M.q: A nursing student must complete at least 120 clinical hours. She has already completed 47.5 hours, and each clinical shift is 7.5 hours long. What is the least number of additional shifts she must complete?
M.w: Write 47.5 + 7.5s ≥ 120. Subtract 47.5: 7.5s ≥ 72.5. Divide by 7.5: s ≥ 9.67. Shifts are whole, so she needs at least 10 (47.5 + 75 = 122.5 hours).

n.0: This rounds 9.67 down. Nine shifts give 47.5 + 67.5 = 115 hours, which is short of 120.
n.1: This divides the full 120 hours by 7.5 and ignores the 47.5 hours already completed.
n.3: Sign error: this adds 47.5 to 120 instead of subtracting it, giving 167.5 ÷ 7.5 ≈ 22.3, then rounds up.

M.q: A dietitian studies whether daily sodium intake affects blood pressure. All participants are 40 to 50 years old, follow the same exercise routine, and take no blood pressure medication. Which are controlled variables in this study? Select all that apply.
o: Blood pressure
Exercise routine
Daily sodium intake
Age range of participants
Medication use
M.w: Controlled variables are factors held the same for everyone so they cannot explain differences in the outcome: the age range, the exercise routine, and medication use.

n.0: Blood pressure is the outcome measured, so it is the dependent variable.
n.2: Sodium intake is the factor being tested, so it is the independent variable.

M.q: Solve for x: (3/4)x - 5 = 13.
M.w: Add 5 to both sides: (3/4)x = 18. Multiply both sides by the reciprocal 4/3: x = 18 × 4/3 = 24. Check: (3/4)(24) - 5 = 18 - 5 = 13.

n.0: This multiplies 18 by 3/4 instead of by its reciprocal, 4/3.
n.2: This multiplies 18 by 4 but does not divide by 3. Multiplying by 4/3 does both.
n.3: Sign error: 5 was subtracted from 13 instead of added, giving (3/4)x = 8.

M.q: A data set of wait times, in minutes, is 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 38. Which statement about the data set is true?
o: The median of the wait times is 20
The mean exceeds the median
The range of the wait times is 23
The mode of the wait times is 2
M.w: Mean = 140 / 7 = 20. Median = 4th value = 18. 20 > 18, so the mean is greater than the median (the 38 pulls the mean up).

n.0: 20 is the mean; the median is the middle (4th) value, 18.
n.2: 38 - 15 = 23 uses the mode as the minimum; the range is 38 - 12 = 26.
n.3: 15 appears twice; the mode is 15, not the number of times it appears.

M.q: A hospital employs 250 nurses, and 38 of them hold a specialty certification. What percent of the nurses hold a specialty certification? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.0.152: Left the answer as a decimal instead of converting to a percent.
tr.84.8: Found the percent of nurses without a certification.

M.q: In a pie chart of a clinic's annual expenses, the medical supplies sector has a central angle of 54°. Medical supplies cost $13,500 for the year. What were the clinic's total annual expenses? Enter the number of dollars only, without commas.

tr.15: the supplies percent, not the total
tr.250: 13,500 / 54, treating the angle as the percent
tr.2025: 13,500 x 0.15, applying the percent instead of dividing by it

M.w: Fraction of the whole: 54 / 360 = 0.15 (15%). Supplies = 0.15 x total, so total = 13,500 / 0.15 = $90,000.

M.q: A travel nurse worked 38.5, 41.2, 39.8, 40.6 and 39.1 hours over five weeks. Which is the best estimate of the total number of hours she worked?
M.w: All five values cluster near 40, so estimate 5 × 40 = 200 hours. (Exact: 199.2 hours.)

n.0: 40 is the typical hours in one week, not the total for all five weeks.
n.2: 220 rounds every value up to the next ten (40 + 50 + 40 + 50 + 40) instead of to the nearest ten.
n.3: 170 truncates each value to the tens place (30 + 40 + 30 + 40 + 30) instead of rounding.

M.q: In a nursing cohort, two-thirds of the students plus 8 more students equals three-fourths of the cohort. How many students are in the cohort? Enter the number of students.

tr.8: Found that 8 students equal 1/12 of the cohort but did not multiply by 12.

M.w: Write (2/3)x + 8 = (3/4)x. Multiply every term by 12: 8x + 96 = 9x. Subtract 8x: x = 96. Check: (2/3)(96) = 64, 64 + 8 = 72, and (3/4)(96) = 72.

M.q: A frequency table shows quiz scores for 20 students: a score of 6, 2 students; 7, 4 students; 8, 4 students; 9, 6 students; 10, 4 students. What is the median quiz score?
M.w: With 20 values, the median is the mean of the 10th and 11th. Running totals: 2, 6, 10, 16, 20. The 10th value is 8 and the 11th is 9, so the median is (8 + 9) / 2 = 8.5.

n.0: 166 / 20 = 8.3 is the mean, not the median.
n.1: 9 is the mode (6 students) and only the 11th value.
n.2: 8 is the middle of the score values 6 to 10 ignoring the frequencies, and it is only the 10th value.

M.q: A pharmacy table lists units on hand and average daily use: Drug A 180 on hand, 12 per day; Drug B 95, 8 per day; Drug C 240, 30 per day; Drug D 130, 9 per day; Drug E 210, 14 per day; Drug F 66, 5 per day. A drug is reordered when it has fewer than 14 days of supply left. Which drugs should be reordered? Select all that apply.
o: Drug C
Drug B
Drug E
Drug D
Drug A
Drug F
M.w: Days of supply = units on hand / daily use. A: 180 / 12 = 15. B: 95 / 8 = 11.9. C: 240 / 30 = 8. D: 130 / 9 = 14.4. E: 210 / 14 = 15. F: 66 / 5 = 13.2. Fewer than 14 days: B, C and F. Drug C has the most units on hand but the shortest supply.

n.2: 210 / 14 = 15 days; the daily use of 14 is not the number of days left.
n.3: 130 / 9 = 14.4 days, just above the 14-day threshold.
n.4: 180 / 12 = 15 days, which is not fewer than 14.

M.q: A 13-foot ladder leans against the wall of a building. The foot of the ladder rests on level ground 5 feet from the base of the wall. How high up the wall does the top of the ladder reach?
o: 4 ft
8 ft
12 ft
M.w: The ladder is the hypotenuse. h² = 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144, so h = 12 ft (a 5-12-13 right triangle).

n.0: This subtracts 5 instead of 5² (169 - 5 = 164, and the square root of 164 is about 12.8).
n.1: This doubles each length instead of squaring it (26 - 10 = 16, and the square root of 16 is 4).
n.2: This subtracts the lengths (13 - 5); the Pythagorean theorem works with the squares of the sides.

M.q: A circular garden has a circumference of 62.8 feet. The gardener needs its area to buy the right amount of mulch. What is the area of the garden? Use 3.14 for pi. Enter the number of square feet.

tr.100: Stopped at r² = 100 without multiplying by pi.
tr.1256: Used the diameter (20 ft) as the radius.
tr.31.4: Multiplied pi by the radius (3.14 × 10) instead of by the radius squared.

M.q: A courier charges 3 times the sum of a package's weight w, in pounds, and 2, plus a $5 handling fee. Which expression gives the charge, in dollars, for one package?
M.w: 'The sum of w and 2' is (w + 2). '3 times the sum' is 3(w + 2). Adding the $5 handling fee gives 3(w + 2) + 5, which simplifies to 3w + 11.

n.0: This multiplies only w by 3. 'Times the sum' needs parentheses so both w and 2 are tripled: 3(w + 2) = 3w + 6.
n.1: This swaps the multiplier and the fee: the sum is multiplied by 3, and the $5 fee is then added.
n.2: This puts the $5 fee inside the parentheses, so the fee is tripled too. The fee is added once, after multiplying.

M.q: A pharmacy technician is sorting five powder samples by mass. The labels use different metric units. Place the samples in order from least mass to greatest mass, starting with the least.
o: 380 mg

M.q: A square patio tabletop is 30 inches on each side. A circular hole with a diameter of 10 inches is cut out of the center for an umbrella pole. What is the area of the tabletop that remains? Use 3.14 for pi. Enter the number of square inches.

tr.586: Used the diameter (10 in) as the radius of the hole (3.14 × 100 = 314).
tr.868.6: Subtracted the hole's circumference (31.4 in) instead of its area.
tr.78.5: Gave the area of the hole instead of the area that remains.

M.w: Square = 30 × 30 = 900 in². Hole: r = 5 in, so A = 3.14 × 5² = 78.5 in². Remaining = 900 - 78.5 = 821.5 in².

M.q: A nurse records a newborn's weight as 7 pounds 13 ounces. The nursery's electronic scale displays weight in ounces. What weight, in ounces, should the scale display for this newborn?
o: 83 oz
97 oz
125 oz
112 oz

n.0: This uses 10 ounces per pound, treating pounds like a decimal unit; 1 lb = 16 oz.
n.1: This uses 12 ounces per pound; 1 lb = 16 oz.
n.3: This converts the 7 pounds (7 × 16 = 112 oz) but does not add the 13 ounces.

M.q: A bag holds 1 1/2 cups of rice. A cook uses 3/4 cup, and then uses 2/3 of the rice that remains. How many cups of rice does the cook use in the second step?
M.w: Remaining after the first step: 1 1/2 - 3/4 = 6/4 - 3/4 = 3/4 cup. Second step: 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2 cup.

n.0: 3/4 cup is what remains after the first step, before the 2/3 is taken.
n.1: 1/4 cup is what is left in the bag after both steps.
n.2: 1 1/8 divides 3/4 by 2/3 instead of multiplying (taking 2/3 of an amount means multiply).

M.q: A family's restaurant bill is $64 before tax. Sales tax is 8.5% of the $64, and the family leaves a 20% tip based on the $64 pre-tax amount. What is the total amount the family pays?

n.0: This calculates the tip on the bill after tax ($69.44 × 1.20), but the tip is based on the $64 pre-tax amount.
n.1: This adds the $5.44 sales tax but leaves out the $12.80 tip.
n.2: This adds the $12.80 tip but leaves out the $5.44 sales tax.

M.q: The trend line for a scatterplot of hours since a dose (x) and drug concentration in the blood, in mcg/mL (y), is y = -1.8x + 24. According to the trend line, after how many hours will the concentration be 9 mcg/mL? Round to the nearest tenth.

tr.7.8: substituting 9 for x (24 - 16.2) instead of for y

M.q: A tablet used for charting shows 92% battery at 1:15 p.m. and 64% battery at 4:45 p.m. What is the average rate at which the battery charge decreased, in percentage points per hour? Enter the number only.

tr.8.48: Wrote 3 hours 30 minutes as 3.3 hours instead of 3.5 hours.

M.w: Change: 92 - 64 = 28 percentage points. Time: 1:15 p.m. to 4:45 p.m. = 3 hours 30 minutes = 3.5 hours. Rate = 28 ÷ 3.5 = 8 percentage points per hour.

M.q:
A stem-and-leaf plot shows the ages of patients seen at a clinic one morning (key: 3 | 1 = 31 years).
2 | 3 7 9
3 | 1 1 4 8
4 | 0 2 5 5 5 6
5 | 2 7
How many patients were older than 30 but younger than 45?
M.w: Ages greater than 30 and less than 45: 31, 31, 34, 38, 40, 42. That is 6 patients. The three 45s are not younger than 45.

n.0: 4 counts only the 3 stem (31, 31, 34, 38) and misses 40 and 42.
n.1: 9 includes the three patients aged 45, who are not younger than 45.
n.3: 10 counts every leaf on the 3 and 4 stems, including 45, 45, 45 and 46.

M.q: A nursing program needs lab coats for 150 students and 8 instructors. It already has 10 new coats in storage, and more coats come only in boxes of 12. What is the least number of boxes the program must order so that everyone gets a coat?
o: 12 boxes
11 boxes
13 boxes
14 boxes
M.w: Coats needed: 150 + 8 = 158. Subtract the 10 in storage: 158 - 10 = 148. Boxes: 148 ÷ 12 = 12.33. Twelve boxes hold only 144 coats, so round up to 13 boxes (156 coats, enough for the 148 still needed).

n.0: 12 boxes rounds 12.33 down; 12 boxes plus storage give 144 + 10 = 154 coats, 4 short.
n.1: 11 boxes subtracts the 8 instructors instead of adding them (150 - 8 - 10 = 132, and 132 ÷ 12 = 11).
n.3: 14 boxes ignores the 10 coats in storage (158 ÷ 12 = 13.17, rounded up), so it orders one box too many.

M.q: A home health nurse drives 24 miles at an average of 32 miles per hour to reach her first patient, then 35 miles at 60 miles per hour to reach her second. What is her total driving time?
o: 1 h 33 min
1 h 17 min
1 h 20 min
45 min
M.w: Time = distance ÷ speed. Leg 1: 24 ÷ 32 = 0.75 h = 45 min. Leg 2: 35 ÷ 60 = 7/12 h = 35 min. Total: 45 + 35 = 80 min = 1 h 20 min.

n.0: 1 h 33 min reads 1.33 hours as 1 hour 33 minutes; 0.33 h is about 20 minutes.
n.1: 1 h 17 min divides the total distance by the average of the two speeds (59 ÷ 46); the legs must be timed separately.
n.3: 45 min is the time for the first leg only.

M.q: A disinfectant is mixed so that 3/40 of the final solution is concentrate and the rest is water. What percent of the final solution is concentrate? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.0.075: Left the answer as a decimal instead of a percent.
tr.0.75: Moved the decimal point only 1 place right.
tr.92.5: Found the percent that is water (100 - 7.5) instead of concentrate.

M.w: 3/40 = 3 ÷ 40 = 0.075. Multiply by 100: 0.075 × 100 = 7.5, so 7.5% of the solution is concentrate.

M.q: An IV of 1,500 mL is ordered to infuse over 12 hours. After 5 hours, 700 mL have infused. At what rate must the rest of the IV run so that it finishes on time? Round to the nearest whole number.
o: 160 mL per hour
114 mL per hour
140 mL per hour
125 mL per hour
M.w: Volume left: 1,500 - 700 = 800 mL. Time left: 12 - 5 = 7 hours. Rate = 800 ÷ 7 = 114.29, which rounds to 114 mL per hour.

n.0: This divides the remaining 800 mL by the 5 hours already used instead of the 7 hours left.
n.2: This is the rate so far, 700 ÷ 5, not the rate needed for the remaining volume.
n.3: This is the original rate, 1,500 ÷ 12. The IV is ahead of schedule (700 mL infused instead of 625 mL), so 125 mL per hour for 7 more hours would deliver 1,575 mL and finish early.

M.q:
A stem-and-leaf plot shows hemoglobin levels, in g/dL, for 11 blood donors (key: 12 | 4 = 12.4).
11 | 2 6 8
12 | 0 4 4 9
13 | 1 5 7
14 | 3
How many donors had a hemoglobin level below 12.5 g/dL?
M.w: Values below 12.5: 11.2, 11.6, 11.8, 12.0, 12.4, 12.4. Each leaf is one donor, so the repeated 4 counts twice: 6 donors.

n.0: 7 includes 12.9, which is above 12.5.
n.1: 5 counts the repeated leaf 12.4 once; each leaf is a separate donor.
n.3: 3 counts only the 11 stem and misses 12.0, 12.4 and 12.4.

M.q: At 6 a.m. the outdoor temperature in Fargo was -7°F. By noon it had risen 15 degrees, and by 9 p.m. it had fallen 11 degrees from the noon reading. What was the temperature at 9 p.m.?
M.w: Start at -7, add the rise and subtract the fall: -7 + 15 = 8, then 8 - 11 = -3°F.

n.0: 11°F treats the starting temperature as +7 (7 + 15 - 11).
n.1: 19°F adds the 11-degree fall instead of subtracting it (8 + 11).
n.2: 3°F drops the negative sign; 8 - 11 is 3 below zero.

M.q: The dose of a medicine varies directly with a patient's body weight. A patient who weighs 60 kg receives 150 mg. What dose, in milligrams, should a patient who weighs 84 kg receive?

tr.107.1: treating it as inverse variation (150 x 60 / 84)
tr.2.5: the constant of variation, not the dose

M.w: Direct variation: dose = k x weight. k = 150 / 60 = 2.5 mg per kg. Dose = 2.5 x 84 = 210 mg.

M.q: A soup recipe that serves 6 people uses 2 1/4 cups of broth. How many cups of broth are needed to make the recipe serve 10 people?
o: 6 1/4 cups
3 3/4 cups
4 1/2 cups
1 7/20 cups
M.w: Set up 2.25/6 = x/10. Cross-multiply: 6x = 22.5, so x = 3.75 = 3 3/4 cups.

n.0: This adds 4 cups for the 4 extra servings instead of scaling by 10/6.
n.2: This doubles the recipe, but 10 servings is 10/6 = 1 2/3 times the recipe, not 2 times.
n.3: This sets up the proportion upside down, multiplying 2 1/4 by 6/10.

S.q: A nurse records a patient's body temperature every 2 hours for 24 hours and wants to show the class how it changed across the day. Which type of graph is the best choice?
o: Histogram
Circle graph
Line graph
Bar graph
S.w: A line graph shows how a continuous variable (temperature) changes over time, with time on the x-axis.

n.0: A histogram shows how often values fall in each interval, which loses the order of the readings in time.
n.1: A circle (pie) graph shows parts of a whole that add to 100%, not change over time.
n.3: A bar graph compares separate categories; it hides the continuous trend between readings.

S.q: A student runs a reaction twice with the same reactant amounts and temperature, adding a catalyst the second time. Which outcome should the student predict for the second run?
o: A faster reaction that forms the same products
A faster reaction that forms different products
A faster reaction that uses up the catalyst
A slower reaction that forms different products
S.w: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the reaction goes faster. It is not consumed and does not change which products form.

n.1: The rate rises, but the products are unchanged; a catalyst does not alter the reaction's outcome.
n.2: A catalyst is regenerated at the end of the reaction; it is not used up as a reactant.
n.3: A catalyst speeds a reaction, and the products stay the same.

S.q: After a large meal, a person's liver and skeletal muscles store excess glucose as a highly branched polysaccharide. Which molecule is formed?
o: Glycogen
Starch
Cellulose
Chitin
S.w: Animals store glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles. Starch is the plant storage form.

n.1: Starch is the storage polysaccharide of plants, not animals.
n.2: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide in plant cell walls.
n.3: Chitin is a structural polysaccharide in fungal walls and insect exoskeletons.

S.q: A swimmer's core temperature falls to 35 degrees C (95 degrees F) in cold water, and her skeletal muscles begin shivering. Which statement best describes the shivering?
o: A receptor response that detects the drop in core temperature
A positive feedback response that amplifies the temperature drop
A control center response that lowers the body's temperature set point
An effector response in negative feedback that generates heat
S.w: Skeletal muscles are effectors. Shivering produces heat that reverses the fall in temperature, so it is a negative feedback response.

n.0: Temperature receptors detect the drop; the shivering muscles produce the response.
n.1: Shivering opposes the drop by generating heat, so it does not amplify the change.
n.2: The control center (hypothalamus) directs shivering to restore the set point, not to lower it.

S.q: A student records the mass of a tiny crystal as 0.004050 g on an analytical balance. How many significant figures does this measurement contain?
S.w: Leading zeros (0.00) are placeholders and never count. The 4 and 5 count, the zero between them counts, and the trailing zero after the decimal point counts: 4, 0, 5, 0 = 4 significant figures.

n.0: This counts the zeros after the decimal point that come before the 4; leading zeros are not significant.
n.1: This drops the final zero; a trailing zero to the right of a decimal point is significant.
n.3: This counts every digit written, including all the leading zeros.
