S.q: A rectangular area on a microscope slide is measured as 2.5 cm by 3.42 cm. A student multiplies to find the area. How should the area be reported with the correct number of significant figures?
o: 8.6 cm²
9 cm²
8.55 cm²
S.w: 2.5 x 3.42 = 8.55. In multiplication, the answer keeps the fewest significant figures of the inputs: 2.5 has 2 and 3.42 has 3, so report 2 significant figures: 8.6 cm².

n.1: This rounds to 1 significant figure; the least precise input (2.5) has 2.
n.2: Adding a trailing zero claims 4 significant figures, more than either measurement supports.
n.3: This keeps 3 significant figures, but 2.5 cm limits the answer to 2.

S.q: Place the regions of the large intestine in the order that undigested material moves through them, starting with the first region after the ileocecal valve.
o: Rectum
Cecum
Descending colon
Ascending colon
Sigmoid colon
Transverse colon
S.w: Material enters the cecum at the ileocecal valve, rises in the ascending colon, crosses in the transverse colon, falls in the descending colon, curves through the sigmoid colon and is stored in the rectum before the anal canal.

S.q: In a drug trial, doses of 10, 20 and 30 mg lowered systolic blood pressure by 5, 10 and 15 mmHg. A student predicts that a 90 mg dose would lower it by 45 mmHg. How should this prediction be evaluated?
o: It extends the trend far past the doses tested, so it is unreliable.
It is reliable, because it lies within the range of the data collected.
It is reliable, because the three data points form a straight line.
It is too low, because drug effects grow exponentially with the dose.
S.w: Predicting beyond the range tested (extrapolation) is unreliable: the trend may level off or reverse at higher doses. The data cover only 10 to 30 mg, so 90 mg is far outside them.

n.1: 90 mg is far outside the tested range of 10 to 30 mg, so the prediction is an extrapolation.
n.2: A straight line within the tested range does not show the trend continues three times beyond it.
n.3: The data rise by a steady 5 mmHg per 10 mg; nothing in them suggests exponential growth.

S.q: After a stroke, Mr. Okafor understands questions but struggles to produce fluent speech. Damage to which area, in which lobe, best explains this?
o: Broca's area in the frontal lobe
Broca's area in the temporal lobe
Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe
Wernicke's area in the frontal lobe
S.w: Two steps: trouble producing speech with comprehension intact points to Broca's area (speech production), and Broca's area lies in the frontal lobe, usually on the left.

n.1: Broca's area is the right area, but it lies in the frontal lobe, not the temporal lobe.
n.2: Wernicke's area handles language comprehension, which is intact here.
n.3: Wernicke's area handles comprehension and lies in the temporal lobe, so both parts are wrong.

S.q: Standing in a cold wind, a hiker begins to shiver. Which statement best explains how shivering helps maintain body temperature?
o: Dermal blood vessels dilate, carrying warm blood out to the skin
Cardiac muscle beats faster, and its extra contractions make the heat
Smooth muscle in vessel walls contracts rhythmically and releases heat
Skeletal muscles contract involuntarily, releasing heat as they use ATP
S.w: Shivering is rapid, involuntary contraction of skeletal muscle triggered by the hypothalamus. Much of the energy released as the muscles use ATP is lost as heat, so heat production rises and body temperature is maintained. Constriction of dermal vessels conserves heat but does not produce it.

n.0: Dilation of dermal vessels sends warm blood to the surface and releases heat; in the cold these vessels constrict to conserve it.
n.1: A faster heartbeat is not shivering; shivering is repeated contraction of the large mass of skeletal muscle, which is the main source of the extra heat.
n.2: Shivering is contraction of skeletal muscle, not vascular smooth muscle; narrowing of dermal vessels conserves heat but is not shivering.

S.q: A patient with type A blood is mistakenly given type B red blood cells and has a transfusion reaction. What causes the reaction?
o: Her anti-B antibodies bind the B antigens on the donor red cells
Her plasma lacks antibodies, so the donor B antigens attack her cells
Her anti-A antibodies bind the A antigens on the donor red cells
Her A antigens bind directly to the B antigens on the donor red cells
S.w: Step 1: type A blood has A antigens on the cells and anti-B antibodies in the plasma. Step 2: donor type B cells carry B antigens, so her anti-B antibodies bind them and destroy the donor cells.

n.1: Type A plasma does contain antibodies (anti-B), and antigens are markers, not attackers.
n.2: Type A blood does not contain anti-A antibodies (they would attack her own cells), and type B cells carry no A antigen.
n.3: Antigens do not bind one another; antibodies bind antigens.

S.q: A short segment of double-stranded DNA contains 4 guanine-cytosine pairs and 6 adenine-thymine pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
S.w: Step 1: G-C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds and A-T pairs have 2. Step 2: (4 x 3) + (6 x 2) = 12 + 12 = 24.

n.0: 30 counts every pair as having 3 hydrogen bonds; A-T pairs have 2.
n.1: 20 counts every pair as having 2 hydrogen bonds; G-C pairs have 3.
n.3: 26 swaps the bond numbers: (4 x 2) + (6 x 3) gives 26.

S.q: A few hours after death, the skeletal muscles of the body become stiff and rigid. Which explanation of this rigor mortis is correct?
o: Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin
Excess acetylcholine keeps restimulating the fibers
Without ATP, myosin heads cannot attach to actin
Without calcium, troponin keeps tropomyosin in place
S.w: Step 1: after death, ATP production stops. Step 2: ATP must bind a myosin head to release it from actin, so the cross-bridges stay locked and the muscles remain rigid.

n.1: Acetylcholine release requires living motor neurons and is cleared by acetylcholinesterase; the stiffness comes from the lack of ATP.
n.2: If myosin could not attach, the muscles would stay limp; the problem is that attached heads cannot let go.
n.3: Tropomyosin blocking actin would prevent cross-bridges and keep muscle relaxed, not rigid.

S.q: Place these substances in order of pH, starting with the most acidic and ending with the most basic.
o: Household ammonia
Stomach acid
Black coffee
Human blood
Pure water
S.w: Approximate pH values: stomach acid 1.5-3.5, black coffee about 5, pure water 7 (neutral), blood 7.35-7.45 (slightly basic) and household ammonia about 11. Lower pH means more acidic.

S.q: Which epidermal cell produces a pigment that absorbs ultraviolet radiation and helps protect the DNA of nearby skin cells from damage?
o: Keratinocyte
Merkel cell
Melanocyte
Langerhans (dendritic) cell
S.w: Melanocytes in the stratum basale make melanin, a pigment that absorbs UV radiation and shields the DNA of surrounding keratinocytes.

n.0: Keratinocytes, the most numerous epidermal cells, make keratin, a tough waterproofing protein rather than a UV-absorbing pigment.
n.1: Merkel cells in the stratum basale act as receptors for light touch.
n.3: Langerhans (dendritic) cells are immune cells in the stratum spinosum that present antigens.

S.q: When the volume of the thoracic cavity increases during inspiration, what happens to the pressure inside the lungs, and which way does air move?
o: Pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, so air flows in
Pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in
Pressure stays equal to atmospheric pressure as air flows in
Pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows out
S.w: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related. Larger thoracic volume means lower intrapulmonary pressure; air flows from high (atmosphere) to low (lungs).

n.0: A larger volume lowers the pressure; higher pressure in the lungs would push air out.
n.2: Air moves only when a pressure gradient exists; equal pressures mean no airflow.
n.3: The pressure change is right, but air moves from high to low pressure, which is into the lungs.

S.q: A histology student is comparing the four basic tissue types. Which feature distinguishes connective tissue from epithelial, muscle and nervous tissue?
o: Cells that generate and conduct electrical impulses
Cells scattered within an extracellular matrix of fibers
Cells joined tightly together with an exposed free surface
Cells that shorten when stimulated to produce movement
S.w: Connective tissue cells are scattered within an extracellular matrix made of ground substance and fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular). In blood, the matrix is fluid plasma.

n.0: Generating and conducting impulses describes the neurons of nervous tissue.
n.2: Tightly joined cells with a free (apical) surface describe epithelial tissue.
n.3: Contractility describes muscle tissue.

S.q: Which statement best describes quiet expiration in a healthy adult at rest?
o: It is passive: the inspiratory muscles relax and the lungs recoil elastically
It is passive: the abdominal muscles relax and the diaphragm flattens out
It is active: the internal intercostals contract and pull the ribs down
It is active: the diaphragm contracts and pushes upward against the lungs
S.w: Quiet expiration is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, the elastic lungs and chest wall recoil, thoracic volume falls and pressure rises above atmospheric, so air flows out.

n.1: A flattening diaphragm enlarges the thorax, which belongs to inspiration, not expiration.
n.2: Internal intercostals are used in forced expiration (coughing, exercise), not quiet breathing.
n.3: The diaphragm relaxes during expiration; when it contracts it flattens downward.

S.q: Silicon and germanium are used in computer chips. Both are shiny, gray solids, yet they shatter when struck and conduct electricity only moderately. To which category of elements do they belong?
o: Nonmetals
Transition metals
Alkaline earth metals
Metalloids
S.w: Metalloids lie along the staircase line between metals and nonmetals and mix their properties: a metallic luster with nonmetal brittleness, and conductivity between the two (semiconductors). Silicon and germanium are classic metalloids.

n.0: Solid nonmetals can be brittle, but they are typically dull and poor conductors (insulators), not shiny semiconductors.
n.1: Transition metals are shiny, but they are malleable rather than brittle and conduct electricity well.
n.2: Alkaline earth metals (group 2) are shiny metals that conduct electricity well, unlike these moderate conductors.

S.q: Three trials of a student's experiment all show that bean seeds soaked overnight sprout faster than dry bean seeds, as her hypothesis predicted. Which conclusion is worded correctly?
o: The data support the hypothesis, which is now a scientific theory.
The data prove the hypothesis for the bean seeds tested.
The data support the hypothesis for seeds of all plant species.
The data support the hypothesis for the bean seeds tested.
S.w: Data support or fail to support a hypothesis; they do not prove it. A sound conclusion also stays within what was tested (bean seeds), and one small experiment does not create a theory.

n.0: A theory is a broad explanation tested many times by many scientists; one student's three trials do not turn a hypothesis into a theory.
n.1: Data support a hypothesis but never prove it; a later replicated result could still contradict it, even for bean seeds.
n.2: Only bean seeds were tested, so extending the result to every plant species generalizes beyond the population studied.

S.q: The reaction 2 NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ releases heat in the forward direction (it is exothermic). If this equilibrium mixture is heated, how will the equilibrium respond?
o: It shifts right, because heating speeds the forward rate
It shifts right, toward N₂O₄, the exothermic direction
It does not shift, because heat affects rate, not equilibrium
It shifts left, toward NO₂, the endothermic direction
S.w: For an exothermic reaction, heat acts like a product. Adding heat is a stress that the system relieves by shifting in the endothermic direction, which is to the left, producing more NO₂.

n.0: Heating speeds both directions, but it speeds the endothermic (reverse) reaction more, so the net shift is left.
n.1: Shifting in the exothermic direction would release even more heat; raising temperature favors the endothermic direction.
n.2: Temperature changes do shift equilibrium; it is a catalyst that leaves the equilibrium position unchanged.

S.q: A beaker of crushed ice at 0 °C is heated steadily on a hot plate. While the ice is melting and some solid is still present, what happens to the temperature of the ice-water mixture?
o: It stays at 0 °C, because the energy breaks attractions between molecules
It rises to 4 °C, where water is densest, before melting is complete
It rises steadily, because the heat raises the molecules' kinetic energy
It falls slightly, because melting releases heat to the surroundings
S.w: During a phase change, the temperature stays constant. The added energy (heat of fusion) goes into breaking the attractions holding molecules in the solid, not into raising their average kinetic energy. This is the flat plateau on a heating curve.

n.1: Water is densest at about 4 °C, but the mixture does not warm above 0 °C until all the ice has melted.
n.2: The temperature rises before and after melting, but not during it; the energy is used to change the state.
n.3: Melting absorbs heat (endothermic). Freezing is the change that releases heat.

S.q: A 30-year-old fractures the tibia in a fall. Place the stages of fracture repair in the order they occur, starting with the first.
o: A bony (hard) callus replaces the soft callus
A hematoma (blood clot) forms at the break
A fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus bridges the gap
Osteoclasts and osteoblasts remodel the bony callus
S.w: Fracture repair runs hematoma, then fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus, then bony (hard) callus, then remodeling, in which osteoclasts remove excess bone and osteoblasts reshape the site toward its original form.

S.q: At rest, a client's heart rate is 80 beats per minute and the stroke volume is 65 mL per beat. What is the cardiac output? Enter your answer in liters per minute, rounded to the nearest tenth.

tr.145: Added heart rate and stroke volume instead of multiplying.
tr.5200: Gave the answer in milliliters per minute; divide by 1,000 to get liters.
tr.0.8: Divided stroke volume by heart rate instead of multiplying.

S.w: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 80 × 65 = 5,200 mL/min. Convert to liters: 5,200 ÷ 1,000 = 5.2 L/min.

S.q: At rest, the inside of a typical neuron is about -70 mV relative to the outside. Which mechanism uses ATP directly to help maintain this resting membrane potential?
o: Na⁺/K⁺ pump moving 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels letting Na⁺ flow in
Ca²⁺ channels letting Ca²⁺ into the axon terminal
Na⁺/K⁺ pump moving 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in
S.w: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in. Together with K⁺ leak channels, this keeps the inside of the resting neuron negative.

n.1: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open at threshold and cause depolarization; they are passive channels, not an ATP-driven pump.
n.2: Ca²⁺ channels at the axon terminal open during synaptic transmission; they do not maintain the resting potential.
n.3: The ratio is reversed: the pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in.

S.q: A normal human sperm cell fertilizes a normal secondary oocyte. Which statement about the chromosomes carried by that sperm is correct?
o: It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, carrying either an X or a Y chromosome
It is diploid, carrying 46 chromosomes including one X and one Y
It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, and the egg's chromosome sets the child's sex
It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, each sperm carrying an X chromosome
S.w: Meiosis makes sperm haploid (n = 23). Each sperm carries either an X or a Y, so the sperm determines the child's sex; the egg carries an X. Fertilization restores the diploid number (2n = 46).

n.1: Gametes are haploid; 46 chromosomes is the diploid number restored at fertilization.
n.2: The egg carries an X in every case, so it is the sperm's X or Y that sets the child's sex.
n.3: It is the egg that carries an X in every case; sperm carry either an X or a Y.

S.q: Sodium, a reactive metal, combines with chlorine, a nonmetal, to form sodium chloride (NaCl), the main salt in normal saline. Which statement correctly describes the bond in NaCl?
o: Covalent, formed as the two atoms share a pair of electrons
Metallic, formed by a sea of electrons around both atoms
Ionic, formed as sodium transfers an electron to chlorine
Ionic, formed as chlorine transfers an electron to sodium
S.w: A metal and a nonmetal with a large difference in electronegativity form an ionic bond. Sodium loses its single valence electron to chlorine, producing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that are held together by electrostatic attraction.

n.0: Sharing electron pairs describes covalent bonds, which form mainly between nonmetals.
n.1: Metallic bonding holds atoms of a metal together; NaCl is a metal combined with a nonmetal.
n.3: The bond is ionic, but the electron moves from the metal (sodium) to the nonmetal (chlorine), not the other way.

S.q: A textbook describes the two strands of a DNA double helix as antiparallel. What does this term mean?
o: The two strands run in opposite directions.
One strand is made of DNA and the other of RNA.
The strands are joined by covalent bonds between bases.
The two strands have exactly the same base sequence.
S.w: Antiparallel means the two strands run in opposite directions: one runs 5' to 3' and its partner runs 3' to 5'.

n.1: Both strands of the double helix are DNA. DNA-RNA pairing happens only briefly during transcription.
n.2: Bases are joined across the strands by hydrogen bonds; that describes bonding, not direction.
n.3: The strands are complementary (A-T, G-C), not identical in sequence.

S.q: A poison control leaflet explains that a few substances can enter the blood directly through the stomach lining, before reaching the small intestine. Which substance is one of these?
o: Alcohol
Vitamin B12
Fatty acids
Amino acids
S.w: The stomach absorbs very little, but some water, alcohol and aspirin can cross its lining. Nutrients are absorbed mainly in the small intestine.

n.1: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum with intrinsic factor, not across the stomach lining.
n.2: Fatty acids are absorbed in the small intestine and enter the lacteals as chylomicrons.
n.3: Amino acids are absorbed into blood capillaries of the small intestine villi.

S.q: During meiosis I in a woman's ovary, the two copies of chromosome 21 fail to separate, and both end up in the egg. A normal sperm fertilizes this egg. What will the zygote most likely have?
o: 47 chromosomes, including three copies of chromosome 21
47 chromosomes, with an XXY set of sex chromosomes
45 chromosomes, with one copy of chromosome 21
45 chromosomes, the pattern seen in Turner syndrome
S.w: Step 1: nondisjunction gives the egg 24 chromosomes, including two copies of chromosome 21. Step 2: adding a normal sperm's 23 gives 47, with three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21, Down syndrome).

n.1: XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) involves the sex chromosomes, but the nondisjunction here involved chromosome 21.
n.2: A zygote with one chromosome 21 would come from an egg that received no copy. Here the egg received both copies.
n.3: Turner syndrome (45,X) is a missing sex chromosome. This egg has an extra chromosome, so the total rises above 46.

S.q: Red blood cells are placed in a salt solution that has a higher solute concentration than the fluid inside the cells. What happens to the cells?
o: Salt moves into the cells until they burst
Water moves out of the cells, and they shrink
Water moves both ways equally, and size holds
Water moves into the cells, and they swell
S.w: In osmosis, water moves across a semipermeable membrane toward the higher solute concentration. The outside solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the cells and they shrink (crenate).

n.0: Osmosis is the movement of water, not salt; the cells lose water and shrink.
n.2: Equal movement both ways describes an isotonic solution, such as 0.9% saline.
n.3: Swelling happens in a hypotonic solution, where the outside solute concentration is lower.

S.q: A student is reviewing how the three ABO alleles (IA, IB and i) interact. Which statement about the ABO blood group system is accurate?
o: IA is dominant over IB, so a person with IAIB is type A.
IA and IB blend by incomplete dominance into type AB.
The i allele is dominant, so type O is the most common.
The i allele is recessive to both the IA and IB alleles.
S.w: ABO shows multiple alleles: IA and IB are codominant with each other, and both are dominant over i. Type O requires ii.

n.0: IA and IB are codominant; a person with IAIB expresses both and is type AB.
n.1: Type AB shows both A and B antigens fully, which is codominance, not a blend.
n.2: i is recessive. A person must have two copies (ii) to be type O.

S.q: A physiology handout lists several ways substances cross cell membranes. Which of these processes require the cell to spend ATP? Select all that apply.
o: Neutrophil engulfing a bacterium
Glucose entering by GLUT carriers
Carbon dioxide leaving a cell
Sodium-potassium pump moving ions
Pancreatic cell secreting an enzyme
Water crossing through aquaporins
S.w: Active transport (the Na⁺/K⁺ pump), endocytosis (phagocytosis by a neutrophil) and exocytosis (enzyme secretion) all use ATP. Diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis are passive.

n.1: Glucose moving down its gradient through GLUT carriers is facilitated diffusion, which needs no ATP.
n.2: CO₂ leaves by simple diffusion down its concentration gradient, with no ATP.
n.5: Water crossing through aquaporins is osmosis, a passive process.

S.q: A patient with a bacterial infection develops a moderate fever. Which statement best describes how the fever arises and how it helps the body?
o: Histamine resets the hypothalamic set point, and moderate heat activates memory cells
Pyrogens reset the hypothalamic set point, and moderate heat inhibits pathogens
Pyrogens reset the pituitary set point, and moderate heat inhibits pathogens
Pyrogens reset the hypothalamic set point, giving an antigen-specific adaptive defense
S.w: Fever is an innate, nonspecific second-line defense. Pyrogens released during infection reset the temperature set point in the hypothalamus, and a moderate rise in body temperature inhibits pathogens.

n.0: Pyrogens, not histamine, reset the set point; histamine drives local inflammation, and memory cells belong to adaptive immunity.
n.2: The body's temperature set point is in the hypothalamus, not the pituitary.
n.3: Fever is innate and nonspecific; it does not target one antigen the way adaptive immunity does.

S.q: The two strands of a DNA double helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases. Which statement about these hydrogen bonds is correct?
o: They are stronger than the covalent bonds within each strand
They form when electrons transfer from hydrogen to nitrogen
They are weaker than the covalent bonds within each strand
They form when hydrogen shares an electron pair with carbon
S.w: Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on another N, O or F atom. They are much weaker than covalent bonds, which is why DNA strands can be separated for replication while each strand's backbone stays intact.

n.0: Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds; that weakness lets the strands unzip.
n.1: Hydrogen bonds involve partial charges, not a transfer of electrons, which would make ions.
n.3: A C-H bond is an ordinary covalent bond. Hydrogen bonds need hydrogen attached to N, O or F.

S.q: Electronegativity is a measure of how strongly an atom attracts the shared electrons in a chemical bond. Which of these elements has the highest electronegativity?
o: Fluorine
Iodine
Oxygen
Francium
S.w: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, so it is highest at the upper right of the table (excluding noble gases). Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

n.1: Iodine is a halogen, but it sits far down group 17; electronegativity decreases down a group.
n.2: Oxygen is highly electronegative but lies one place left of fluorine in period 2, so it is slightly lower.
n.3: Francium, at the lower left of the table, has one of the lowest electronegativities of all elements.

S.q: A traveler returns from a tropical region with cycles of fever and chills and is diagnosed with malaria. Which statement correctly identifies the cause and how it spread?
o: A bacterium, spread through contaminated drinking water
A bacterium, spread by the bite of infected deer ticks
A virus, spread by the bite of Anopheles mosquitoes
A protozoan, spread by the bite of Anopheles mosquitoes
S.w: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium, a single-celled eukaryote. The female Anopheles mosquito is the vector that carries it, not the cause.

n.0: Malaria is vector-borne; waterborne protozoan illness is giardiasis.
n.1: Ticks spread Lyme disease, caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, not malaria.
n.2: The mosquito is the correct vector, but the pathogen is a protozoan, not a virus.

S.q: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum. Which hormone does the corpus luteum mainly secrete, and what is its main effect on the uterus?
o: Progesterone, which keeps the endometrium in its secretory state
Estrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium after menstruation
FSH, which prepares the endometrium for implantation
Progesterone, which stimulates contractions of the myometrium
S.w: The corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone (plus some estrogen). Progesterone maintains the thickened, secretory endometrium and relaxes the myometrium, preparing the uterus for implantation.

n.1: Rebuilding the endometrium in the proliferative phase is driven by estrogen from growing follicles before ovulation.
n.2: FSH is an anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates follicles; the corpus luteum does not secrete it.
n.3: Progesterone relaxes the myometrium; oxytocin is the hormone that stimulates uterine contractions.

S.q: The renal corpuscle is the part of the nephron where blood is first filtered. Which two structures together make up the renal corpuscle?
o: Glomerulus and proximal convoluted tubule
Glomerular capsule and nephron loop
Afferent and efferent arterioles
Glomerulus and glomerular capsule
S.w: The renal corpuscle is the glomerulus (capillary tuft) surrounded by the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule. Filtration happens there, not in the tubule.

n.0: The proximal convoluted tubule follows the capsule; it is part of the renal tubule, not the corpuscle.
n.1: The nephron loop (loop of Henle) is part of the tubule and lies mainly in the medulla.
n.2: These arterioles supply and drain the glomerulus but are not the corpuscle itself.

S.q: A routine blood test shows that a patient's calcium level has dropped below its normal range. Which responses would be expected as the body restores it? Select all that apply.
o: Increased secretion of parathyroid hormone
Increased loss of calcium from the kidneys into the urine
Increased deposition of calcium into the bone matrix
More active vitamin D, so the gut absorbs more calcium
Increased calcitonin secretion from the thyroid C cells
Increased osteoclast activity releasing calcium from bone
S.w: Low blood calcium triggers PTH release. PTH stimulates osteoclasts to release calcium from bone, makes the kidneys keep calcium and activates vitamin D so the gut absorbs more calcium.

n.1: PTH makes the kidneys keep calcium, so urinary calcium loss would fall, not rise.
n.2: Depositing calcium into bone lowers blood calcium; that is the calcitonin response to high calcium.
n.4: Calcitonin is released when blood calcium is high and lowers it, so its secretion would fall.

S.q: A tissue sample taken just beneath the epidermis contains blood vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles and a dense mesh of collagen and elastin fibers. Which layer and tissue type does it show?
o: Smooth muscle tissue of the dermis
Connective tissue of the dermis
Epithelial tissue of the epidermis
Adipose tissue of the hypodermis
S.w: The dermis lies beneath the epidermis and is connective tissue: areolar in the papillary layer and dense irregular in the reticular layer, rich in collagen (strength) and elastin (stretch), with vessels, nerves, follicles and glands.

n.0: The dermis does contain tiny arrector pili muscles, but its main tissue is connective tissue, not smooth muscle.
n.2: The epidermis is avascular stratified squamous epithelium; it has no blood vessels or collagen mesh.
n.3: The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and is mostly fat with areolar tissue, not a dense collagen and elastin mesh.

S.q: A website claims that an herbal tea shortens colds. It cites a celebrity endorsement and reviews from 12 happy customers. Which additional evidence would most strengthen the claim?
o: A randomized trial comparing the tea with a look-alike placebo tea
A survey finding that tea buyers report shorter colds than nonbuyers
A trial in which 300 people with colds all drank the tea and got better
A statement from a physician who recommends the tea to her patients
S.w: Only a controlled experiment can establish cause and effect. Randomly assigning people with colds to the tea or a look-alike placebo makes the groups alike except for the tea, so a difference in cold length can be credited to it.

n.1: A survey is observational: buyers chose the tea themselves and self-report their colds, so it shows an association at best, not cause.
n.2: With no comparison group, there is no way to tell whether the colds would have ended just as fast without the tea.
n.3: An authority's recommendation is not evidence; the claim still has to be tested against a control.

S.q: How are the sutures that join the cranial bones of an adult skull classified, both by structure and by the amount of movement they allow?
o: Cartilaginous joints that are slightly movable
Cartilaginous joints that are immovable
Fibrous joints that are slightly movable
Fibrous joints that are immovable
S.w: Sutures are fibrous joints: the bones are held together by short connective tissue fibers with no joint cavity. Functionally they are synarthroses (immovable).

n.0: Slightly movable cartilaginous joints (symphyses) include the pubic symphysis and the intervertebral discs.
n.1: Immovable cartilaginous joints (synchondroses) include the epiphyseal plate and the first rib-sternum joint, not sutures.
n.2: A slightly movable fibrous joint is a syndesmosis, such as the distal tibiofibular joint; sutures are immovable.

S.q: A plastic bead has a mass of 12 g and a volume of 15 mL. It is dropped into a beaker of water, which has a density of 1.0 g/mL. What happens to the bead, and why?
o: It floats, because its density is 0.8 g/mL
It sinks, because its density is 1.8 g/mL
It sinks, because its density is 1.25 g/mL
It floats, because its density is 0.08 g/mL
S.w: Step 1: density = mass / volume = 12 g / 15 mL = 0.8 g/mL. Step 2: an object less dense than the fluid it is placed in floats; 0.8 g/mL is less than water's 1.0 g/mL, so the bead floats.

n.1: 1.8 g/mL comes from adding mass and volume before dividing; density is simply 12 / 15.
n.2: 1.25 g/mL comes from dividing volume by mass (15 / 12). Density is mass divided by volume.
n.3: The bead does float, but 0.08 g/mL is a decimal-place slip; 12 / 15 = 0.8.

S.q: Researchers test a new mouthwash. Group A rinses with 10 mL of it, Group B rinses with 20 mL, and Group C rinses with 10 mL of an identical-looking liquid with no active ingredient. Which is the control group?
o: Group A, which receives the standard dose
Group B, which receives the largest dose
All three groups, since rinse time is the same
Group C, which receives the inactive liquid
S.w: The control group does not receive the treatment and serves as the baseline. Group C receives a placebo, an inactive look-alike, so differences in the other groups can be credited to the active ingredient.

n.0: Group A receives the active treatment, so it is an experimental group.
n.1: The group with the most treatment is still an experimental group, not the control.
n.2: Keeping rinse time the same makes it a controlled variable; controlled variables are not the control group.

S.q: A student is comparing a typical plant cell with a typical animal cell. Which structures are found in the plant cell but not in the animal cell? Select all that apply.
o: Mitochondria for respiration
Ribosomes that make proteins
Large central vacuole
Chloroplasts
Centrioles near the nucleus
Cell wall made of cellulose
S.w: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole that animal cells lack. Both cell types have mitochondria and ribosomes.

n.0: Plant cells have mitochondria too; they respire as well as photosynthesize.
n.1: Ribosomes are found in every cell, plant, animal and prokaryotic.
n.4: Centrioles are usually found in animal cells, not plant cells, so they are the reverse of what is asked.

S.q: A patient with lactose intolerance makes too little lactase. When lactase does digest lactose, which two monosaccharides are released?
o: Glucose and galactose
Galactose and fructose
Glucose and glucose
Glucose and fructose
S.w: Lactose (milk sugar) = glucose + galactose. Lactase hydrolyzes it into those two monosaccharides.

n.1: Galactose + fructose is not one of the common dietary disaccharides.
n.2: Glucose + glucose make maltose.
n.3: Glucose + fructose make sucrose (table sugar).

S.q: A student writes: "All enzymes are proteins. Amylase is an enzyme. Therefore, amylase is a protein." Which statement correctly describes this reasoning?
o: Deductive; the conclusion must be true if the premises are true.
Inductive; the conclusion is probable but could be overturned.
Inductive; the conclusion follows from a general premise.
Deductive; the conclusion is a likely pattern drawn from cases.
S.w: Deductive reasoning moves from a general premise to a specific conclusion. If the premises are true, the conclusion is certain.

n.1: Probable conclusions that can be overturned describe inductive reasoning from cases; this argument starts from a general rule.
n.2: Reasoning from a general premise to a specific case is deductive, not inductive.
n.3: Drawing a pattern from cases is inductive; this argument applies a general rule to one case.

S.q: Place the stages of viral replication in the order they occur when an influenza virus infects a host cell, starting with the first.
o: New virus particles are assembled.
The virus attaches to receptors on the host cell.
New virus particles are released from the cell.
The viral genome is copied and viral proteins are made.
The virus or its genome enters the host cell.
S.w: Viruses replicate only inside host cells: attachment -> entry -> copying of the viral genome and synthesis of viral proteins on the host's ribosomes -> assembly -> release.

S.q: A student has a stained cheek-cell slide in focus under the low-power objective of a compound light microscope and then rotates to the high-power objective. Which next step is correct technique?
o: Lower the stage fully and refocus with the coarse knob
Raise the stage with the coarse knob until it nears the slide
Sharpen the image with the coarse adjustment knob
Sharpen the image with the fine adjustment knob
S.w: Focus is found first on low power with the coarse knob. Once on high power, the objective sits very close to the slide, so the image is sharpened with the fine adjustment knob.

n.0: Starting over with the coarse knob is unnecessary; a microscope that was in focus on low power needs a fine adjustment on high power.
n.1: Moving the stage up with the coarse knob on high power risks the objective striking the slide.
n.2: The coarse knob moves the stage in large steps; on high power it can drive the objective into the slide and break it.

E.q: A pharmacy intern is drafting a patient handout. Which sentence contains an inappropriate shift in pronoun person?
o: We volunteers should bring our badges to every shift this month.
Applicants should check their email often, since the school sends updates there.
If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember it.
When one reads a drug label, you should check the expiration date first.
E.w: "One" is third person, but "you" is second person. Keep one point of view: "When you read a drug label, you should..."

n.0: This sentence stays in first person plural: "we" and "our."
n.1: This sentence is consistent: "applicants" and "their" are both third person plural.
n.2: This sentence stays in second person throughout ("you" and the implied "you" of "take").

E.q: Which working thesis needs revision because it states a fact rather than an arguable claim?
o: Bike lanes are the most cost-effective way for cities to cut traffic injuries.
Twelve-hour nursing shifts do more harm than good for patient safety.
Requiring a CPR course for graduation would make high schools safer places.
The CDC recommends that adults get at least seven hours of sleep each night.
E.w: A thesis must take a position that a reader could dispute. What the CDC recommends can be checked in a single source, so this sentence reports a fact and leaves the essay nothing to argue. The other three make judgments (more harm than good, most cost-effective, would make schools safer) that a writer would have to support.

n.0: Calling bike lanes "the most cost-effective" option is an evaluation that others could challenge with other measures, so it is arguable.
n.1: Whether long shifts do "more harm than good" is a judgment that readers could dispute, so it is an arguable claim.
n.2: Whether a CPR requirement "would make" schools safer is a debatable prediction about a policy, so it is arguable.

E.q: A student writing a lab report adds prefixes to base words. Which word correctly keeps every letter of both the prefix and the root?
o: disatisfied
imature
unnecessary
mispell
E.w: Adding a prefix does not change the spelling of the root: un + necessary = "unnecessary", with both n's kept.

n.0: Dis + satisfied keeps both s's: "dissatisfied".
n.1: Im + mature keeps both m's: "immature".
n.3: Mis + spell keeps both s's: "misspell".

E.q: Rachel's thesis states that community gardens improve neighborhood health by increasing access to fresh produce, encouraging exercise, and building social ties. Which topic sentence best fits her second body paragraph?
o: Friendships formed in community gardens can last for years.
Many cities have started community gardens in empty lots.
Community gardens make fresh produce easier for families to get.
Community gardens also give residents a reason to stay active.
E.w: Body paragraphs usually follow the order of the points previewed in the thesis. The second point is exercise, so the second body paragraph's topic sentence should introduce physical activity.

n.0: Social ties are the thesis's third point, so this belongs to the third body paragraph.
n.1: This is general background that does not develop any of the thesis's three points.
n.2: Access to produce is the thesis's first point, so it belongs to the first body paragraph.

E.q: A lab report described the patient's red blood cells as macrocytic. Using both the prefix and the root, what does macrocytic describe?
o: Cells that are smaller than normal
More cells than normal
Cells that are larger than normal
Fewer cells than normal
E.w: Step 1: macro- means large. Step 2: cyt/o means cell. Macrocytic therefore describes cells that are larger than normal.

n.0: Smaller than normal would be microcytic; micro- means small, the opposite of macro-.
n.1: macro- refers to size, not number; many is multi- or poly-.
n.3: A shortage of cells would use the suffix -penia (deficiency), not macro-.

E.q: A charge nurse is reviewing statements in a staff training packet. Which of the following is a complete sentence?
o: The nurse who works nights trained the new aide.
Because the nurse who works nights trained the aide.
Running to the clinic before the nurse's night shift.
The nurse who works nights and trains the new aides.
E.w: "The nurse ... trained the new aide" has a subject (nurse), a main verb (trained) and a complete thought; "who works nights" is a relative clause inside it.

n.1: "Because" makes the whole word group a dependent clause, which cannot stand alone.
n.2: This is a participial phrase with no subject and no main verb.
n.3: The verbs "works" and "trains" both belong to the relative clause beginning with "who", so "The nurse" has no main verb: a fragment.

E.q: Read the paragraph. (1) When flu season began, the clinic extended its hours. (2) Patients could visit on weekday evenings or on Saturday mornings. (3) The clinic hired two nurses and the staff shared the extra shifts. (4) By March, waiting times had dropped. Which sentence needs a comma added?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
E.w: Sentence 3 joins two independent clauses (The clinic hired two nurses / the staff shared the extra shifts) with "and", so a comma is needed before "and". Without it, a reader first takes "two nurses and the staff" as one object.

n.0: Sentence 1 already has the comma after its introductory clause.
n.1: Sentence 2 has one clause; "or" joins two phrases, so no comma is needed.
n.3: Sentence 4 already has its comma after the introductory phrase.

E.q: An instructor is checking sentences from student case studies. Which sentences use modifiers correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The pharmacist spoke so quietly that the patient asked her to repeat herself.
To pass the licensing exam, careful studying is needed.
Nearly all of the students passed the skills check on the first try.
Of the two job offers, Darnell accepted the best one.
Having finished her charting, Mia clocked out and drove home.
E.w: Mia is the one who finished charting; "quietly" is an adverb modifying "spoke"; "nearly" sits right before "all," the word it limits.

n.1: The infinitive phrase dangles: "studying" cannot pass an exam. A person must be the subject: "To pass the exam, you need to study carefully."
n.3: Two offers call for the comparative "the better one," not the superlative "best."

E.q: A student is grouping health-related words by their Greek and Latin roots. Which words contain a root meaning "write" or "record"? Select all that apply.
o: dictionary
spectator
biography
prescription
transportation
mammogram
E.w: script (prescription) means write, gram (mammogram) means write or record, and graph (biography) means write.

n.0: dict (dictionary) means say, not write.
n.1: spect (spectator) means look.

E.q: A student is writing a history paper about nursing. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: During the Civil War, many irish immigrants served as nurses.
During the civil war, many Irish immigrants served as nurses.
During the Civil War, many Irish Immigrants served as nurses.
During the Civil War, many Irish immigrants served as nurses.
E.w: Named historical events (the Civil War) and nationalities (Irish) are proper nouns; general nouns such as immigrants are lowercase.

n.0: Nationalities are proper adjectives, so "Irish" is capitalized.
n.1: The name of a specific historical event is capitalized: "Civil War".
n.2: "Immigrants" is a common noun and is lowercase.

E.q: Jasmine is sending a quick text message to a close friend to confirm their lunch plans for today. Which message best fits this audience and purpose?
o: Please be advised that I will attend our scheduled lunch at noon.
Sounds good! See you at noon at the taco place.
Maybe lunch sometime this week? Let me know what works for you.
I am writing to confirm that I will meet you for lunch at noon today.
E.w: Register should match the audience. A text to a close friend is informal: short, friendly and conversational.

n.0: "Please be advised" is a formal business phrase that sounds cold in a message to a friend.
n.2: The casual tone fits, but the message fails the purpose: it does not confirm today's lunch plans.
n.3: "I am writing to confirm" is formal letter language, too stiff for a quick text to a close friend.

E.q: A community clinic posts a flyer for free antenatal classes on Tuesday evenings. Based on the prefix, during what period of time are the classes meant to help parents?
o: After the baby is born
During labor and delivery
In the baby's first month
Before the baby is born
E.w: ante- means before and natal refers to birth, so antenatal classes are for the period before the baby is born (the same meaning as prenatal).

n.0: After birth would be postnatal; post- means after.
n.1: ante- means before, not during; during would use intra-.
n.2: The newborn period is neonatal (neo- = new), not antenatal.

E.q: Read the paragraph from a clinic newsletter. (1) The Riverside Clinic opened a second location this spring. (2) Its new site offers evening hours for working families. (3) Patients may book appointments at either location online. (4) Dr. Liu and myself will divide our time between the two offices. Which sentence contains a pronoun error?
o: Sentence 4
Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Sentence 2
E.w: In sentence 4, "myself" is part of the subject and has no antecedent; the subjective case is needed: "Dr. Liu and I will divide our time."

n.1: Sentence 3 has no pronoun error; "either location" is singular and correctly used.
n.2: Sentence 1 contains no pronoun error; it has no pronoun at all.
n.3: "Its" is the correct possessive for the clinic (one organization), with no apostrophe.

E.q: A nutrition handout reads: "Some common foods are high in hidden sodium. ___, a single serving of some canned soups contains more than a third of the recommended daily limit." Which transition best completes the handout?
o: Nevertheless
For example
In conclusion
Likewise
E.w: Canned soup is a specific case of a food with hidden sodium, so the second sentence illustrates the first. "For example" introduces an illustration.

n.0: "Nevertheless" signals contrast, but the second sentence supports the first rather than opposing it.
n.2: "In conclusion" signals a summary, but the second sentence is a specific detail.
n.3: "Likewise" compares two similar ideas, but the soup is an instance of the first claim, not a parallel claim.

E.q: A prenursing student is describing her grades in an application essay. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: She passed Biology 101, but her English and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed biology 101, but her English and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed Biology 101, but her english and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed Biology 101, but her English and Chemistry grades were lower.
E.w: A specific numbered course is a proper noun (Biology 101). General school subjects are lowercase (chemistry), except languages, which are always capitalized (English).

n.1: A specific course name with a number is capitalized: "Biology 101".
n.2: Languages are proper nouns, so "English" is capitalized even as a subject.
n.3: "Chemistry" is a general subject here, not a course title, so it is lowercase.

E.q: Read the sentence: "Walking every day lowers blood pressure." How does the phrase "Walking every day" function?
o: As an infinitive phrase acting as an adverb
As the main verb of the sentence
As a gerund phrase acting as a noun
As a participial phrase acting as an adjective
E.w: "Walking every day" is the subject of the verb "lowers". An -ing verbal used as a noun is a gerund, so this is a gerund phrase acting as a noun.

n.0: An infinitive phrase begins with "to" (to walk).
n.1: The main verb is "lowers"; an -ing word without a helping verb cannot be the main verb.
n.3: A participial phrase modifies a noun; this phrase is itself the subject.

E.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the instruction? "The respiratory therapist will ____ you to take a deep ____ before you exhale slowly."
o: advise; breathe
advice; breathe
advice; breath
advise; breath
E.w: "Advise" is the verb (will advise you); "breath" is the noun (a deep breath). "Advice" and "breathe" are the noun and verb forms of the other pair.

n.0: After "a deep" a noun is needed: "breath". "Breathe" is a verb.
n.1: Both are reversed: the verb is "advise" and the noun is "breath".
n.2: After "will" a verb is needed: "advise". "Advice" is a noun.

E.q: A student is writing up a chemistry lab for a formal report. Which sentence uses the most precise wording?
o: The sample was heated for 10 minutes until it reached 80 degrees Celsius.
The sample was heated briefly until it reached a high temperature.
The sample was heated for several minutes until it reached 80 degrees Celsius.
The sample was heated for 10 minutes until it became very hot.
E.w: Precise word choice gives exact, specific information. A lab report should state measured values, not vague impressions.

n.1: "Briefly" and "a high temperature" sound formal but give no measurable information.
n.2: The temperature is exact, but "several minutes" is vague; a lab report needs the measured time.
n.3: The time is exact, but "very hot" is vague; a lab report needs the measured temperature.

E.q: A nursing student is reviewing sentence structure before the TEAS. Which of the following is a complex sentence?
o: Although she studied all week, Rosa felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week and felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week, yet she felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week; she still felt nervous before the exam.
E.w: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. "Although she studied all week" is dependent (it begins with a subordinating conjunction); "Rosa felt nervous before the exam" is independent.

n.1: One subject with two verbs (studied and felt) is a simple sentence with a compound predicate.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by a comma and "yet" make a compound sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon make a compound sentence.

E.q: A student is building a formal outline for a paper on nurse burnout. Place the outline labels in order from the broadest level to the most specific, starting with the broadest.
o: I.
a.
A.
E.w: A formal outline uses Roman numerals (I.) for main points, capital letters (A.) for supporting ideas, Arabic numerals (1.) for details under those ideas, and lowercase letters (a.) for the most specific subpoints.

E.q: After a long flight, a patient developed pain and redness in her calf, and an ultrasound confirmed thrombophlebitis. Using all of its word parts, what does thrombophlebitis mean?
o: Vein hardening caused by a blood clot
Surgical removal of a clot in a vein
Vein inflammation with a blood clot
Artery inflammation with a blood clot
E.w: Step 1: thromb/o means clot and phleb/o means vein. Step 2: -itis means inflammation. Together: inflammation of a vein associated with a blood clot.

n.0: Hardening is -sclerosis; -itis means inflammation.
n.1: Removal is -ectomy (thrombectomy); -itis means inflammation.
n.3: Artery is arteri/o; phleb/o means vein.

E.q: Read the sentence from a pharmacy incident report: "If the order had been clearer, the pharmacy could of filled it on time." Which revision corrects the verb error?
o: Change "could of filled" to "could have filled" and "had been" to "would have been."
Change "could of filled" to "could have filled."
Change "had been" to "was."
Change "could of filled" to "could had filled."
E.w: "Could of" is a mishearing of "could've." The correct form is "could have" + past participle: "could have filled."

n.0: This fixes "could of" but adds a new error: the if-clause of a past unreal condition takes "had been," not "would have been."
n.2: "Had been" is correct for a past condition that did not happen, and the "could of" error would remain.
n.3: "Could" is a helping verb and must be followed by the base form "have"; "could had filled" is ungrammatical.

E.q: A tall, thin teenager arrived at the emergency department short of breath, and a chest X-ray confirmed a pneumothorax. Based on its word parts, what is a pneumothorax?
o: Pain in the chest wall
Inflammation of a lung
Air in the chest cavity
A surgical cut into the chest
E.w: pneum/o means air or lung and thorac/o means chest, so a pneumothorax is air in the chest cavity (around the lung).

n.0: Pain would need a pain suffix such as -algia or -dynia.
n.1: Inflammation would need -itis (as in pneumonitis).
n.3: A surgical cut would need -otomy (thoracotomy).

E.q: A nursing journal editor is checking sentences in a research article. Which sentences use bias-free language? Select all that apply.
o: The study enrolled 50 adults confined to wheelchairs.
The study included 40 people with epilepsy.
The study enrolled 50 adults who use wheelchairs.
The new nurse manager, a woman in her 30s, was surprisingly organized.
Each server at the hospital cafe received a holiday bonus.
E.w: Bias-free language puts the person first ("adults who use wheelchairs," "people with epilepsy") and uses gender-neutral titles ("server").

n.0: "Confined to wheelchairs" treats the wheelchair as a limit rather than a tool; use "who use wheelchairs."
n.3: Mentioning gender and age is unnecessary here, and "surprisingly" implies a stereotype.

E.q: Read the paragraph from a study-skills guide. (1) Many students believe that cramming the night before an exam is effective. (2) Therefore, research shows that spacing study sessions over several days leads to better recall. (3) For example, students who reviewed material on four separate days remembered more a week later. (4) Overall, spaced practice is a better use of study time than cramming. Which sentence uses an illogical transition?
o: Sentence 2
Sentence 4
Sentence 3
Sentence 1
E.w: Sentence 2 contradicts the belief in sentence 1, so it needs a contrast transition such as "However," not the cause-and-effect "Therefore."

n.1: "Overall" correctly signals a summary of the paragraph's point.
n.2: "For example" correctly introduces a specific study that illustrates sentence 2.
n.3: Sentence 1 has no transition; it introduces the belief the paragraph will challenge.

E.q: Read the paragraph from a patient success story. (1) Hoping to lower her blood pressure, Mrs. Diaz began walking every morning. (2) She walked more slowly than her neighbor but went farther. (3) After three weeks, her readings were lower than before. (4) Encouraged by the results, the walks became longer. Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
E.w: In sentence 4, "Encouraged by the results" is followed by "the walks," so the walks seem encouraged. Fix: "Encouraged by the results, Mrs. Diaz made her walks longer."

n.0: "Lower" correctly compares two things (readings now and before); there is no introductory modifier to dangle.
n.1: "Hoping to lower her blood pressure" is followed by "Mrs. Diaz," the person who was hoping, so the modifier is correct.
n.3: "More slowly" correctly compares two people with an adverb, and "farther" correctly refers to physical distance.

E.q: A chest X-ray and an echocardiogram both showed cardiomegaly in a patient with long-term high blood pressure. Based on its word parts, what does cardiomegaly mean?
o: Hardening of the heart
Narrowing of the heart valves
Enlargement of the heart
Softening of the heart
E.w: cardi/o means heart and -megaly means enlargement, so cardiomegaly is an enlarged heart.

n.0: Hardening is -sclerosis.
n.1: Narrowing is -stenosis (as in aortic stenosis).
n.3: Softening is -malacia.

E.q: A charge nurse is writing a reminder about patient safety bands. Which sentence uses commonly confused words correctly?
o: All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
E.w: "Except" means excluding (all except Mr. Ito); "lose" means to misplace (not to lose their wristbands). "Loose" means not tight.

n.0: "Loose" is an adjective meaning not tight; misplacing something is "lose".
n.1: Both are wrong: excluding someone is "except", and misplacing something is "lose".
n.2: "Accept" means to receive; excluding someone requires "except".

E.q: While revising, Malik notices that his conclusion introduces a new statistic about hospital costs that appears nowhere else in his essay. What is the best revision?
o: Move the statistic to a body paragraph and restate the thesis instead
Add two more statistics so the conclusion fully develops the point
Keep the statistic so the essay ends with its strongest new evidence
Change the statistic into a question to leave readers thinking
E.w: A conclusion restates the thesis in new words and sums up; it should not introduce new evidence. Evidence belongs in a body paragraph that supports the related point.

n.1: Adding more new evidence makes the problem worse by turning the conclusion into another body paragraph.
n.2: New evidence in the conclusion is undeveloped and breaks the conclusion's job of wrapping up.
n.3: Rewording the statistic as a question still introduces new material in the conclusion and leaves the evidence unsupported.

E.q: Mr. Brooks is writing a letter to a hospital about a long wait in its emergency department. Which sentence has the most appropriate tone for his purpose?
o: Thanks a lot for the lovely four-hour wait; I really enjoyed it.
I waited four hours with a broken wrist and would like to know why.
I am sure the department was busy, so please disregard my concerns.
Your staff obviously could not care less about patients like me.
E.w: A complaint letter should be firm, specific and courteous: state what happened and what you want.

n.0: Sarcasm is unprofessional and can be misread, so it weakens the complaint.
n.2: This polite sentence cancels the complaint, so it fails the writer's purpose.
n.3: The angry, accusing tone is likely to make the reader defensive rather than helpful.

E.q: A physician's note must use standard plural forms. Which sentence uses the correct plural of every noun?
o: Both diagnosis were confirmed after the two analyses.
Both diagnoses were confirmed after the two analyses.
Both diagnosises were confirmed after the two analyses.
Both diagnoses were confirmed after the two analysises.
E.w: Greek-origin nouns ending in -is form the plural by replacing -is with -es: diagnosis becomes "diagnoses" and analysis becomes "analyses" (like crisis, crises).

n.0: "Diagnosis" is the singular form, but "both" and "were" require the plural "diagnoses".
n.2: The -is ending is replaced, not kept: the plural of diagnosis is "diagnoses", not "diagnosises".
n.3: The -is ending is replaced, not kept: the plural of analysis is "analyses", not "analysises".

E.q: To find ideas for an article on teen vaping, Rosa writes six headings at the top of her page: Who? What? When? Where? Why? How? She then jots answers under each one. Which stage and technique is she using?
o: Drafting, using freewriting
Prewriting, using outlining
Prewriting, using questioning
Revising, using peer feedback
E.w: Rosa is still generating ideas before writing, so she is prewriting. Asking who, what, when, where, why and how is the questioning technique (the reporter's questions).

n.0: Freewriting is nonstop writing for a set time, and Rosa is not drafting paragraphs; she is answering six set questions.
n.1: Outlining organizes ideas into a hierarchy of main points and subpoints; Rosa is producing ideas, not ranking them.
n.3: Revising improves an existing draft; Rosa has no draft yet, and she is not responding to a reviewer.

E.q: Read the paragraph. (1) Telehealth visits have grown quickly over the past decade. (2) These video appointments can save patients long drives and time off work. (3) However, telehealth does not suit every patient. (4) People without reliable internet may struggle to connect. Where should this sentence be placed? "For example, a farmer who lives an hour from town can see a provider without leaving work."
o: After sentence 1
After sentence 3
After sentence 4
After sentence 2
E.w: An example belongs right after the claim it illustrates. The farmer shows how video visits save long drives and time off work (sentence 2).

n.0: The example is about saving travel and work time, not about how quickly telehealth has grown.
n.1: Placed here, the example would contradict the claim that telehealth does not suit every patient.
n.2: Placed here, a success story would contradict the point about people who struggle to connect.

E.q: Read the sentence: "The nurse carefully explained the very complex procedure." Which word is an adverb that modifies an adjective?
o: complex
explained
very
carefully
E.w: "Very" is an adverb that modifies the adjective "complex", telling how complex the procedure is.

n.0: "Complex" is the adjective being modified; it describes the noun "procedure".
n.1: "Explained" is the verb of the sentence.
n.3: "Carefully" is an adverb, but it modifies the verb "explained", not an adjective.

E.q: A nurse is writing patient instructions and wants every line to be a complete sentence. Which of the following is a complete sentence?
o: Please sign the consent form before the procedure.
The consent form that was signed before the procedure.
Since the consent form was signed before the procedure.
Signing the consent form before the procedure.
E.w: An imperative sentence is complete even though its subject (you) is not stated: "[You] Please sign the consent form."

n.1: "That was signed ..." is a relative clause describing the form; the subject "The consent form" has no main verb.
n.2: "Since" makes this a dependent clause, which cannot stand alone.
n.3: This is a gerund phrase with no main verb.

E.q: A family member is repeating a doctor's instruction and asking a question about it. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Did the doctor really say "no visitors."
Did the doctor really say "no visitors?"
Did the doctor really say "no visitors"?
Did the doctor really say "no visitors".
E.w: The whole sentence is a question, but the quoted words are not. A question mark that belongs to the whole sentence goes outside the closing quotation mark.

n.0: The sentence is a direct question, so it must end with a question mark.
n.1: The quoted words "no visitors" are not a question, so the question mark does not belong inside the quotation marks.
n.3: The sentence is a direct question, so it must end with a question mark, not a period.

E.q: A receptionist is recording a phone call. Which sentence uses end punctuation correctly?
o: The patient asked, "Whether the clinic would be open on Monday?"
The patient asked whether the clinic would be open on Monday.
The patient asked whether the clinic would be open on Monday?
The patient asked, whether the clinic would be open on Monday.
E.w: This is an indirect question: it reports what was asked without quoting the exact words, so it ends with a period and takes no comma or quotation marks.

n.0: These are not the patient's exact words, so quotation marks are wrong.
n.2: An indirect question is a statement, so it ends with a period, not a question mark.
n.3: No comma separates the verb "asked" from the clause that is its object.
